Maths in the Asia Pacific 
© Paul Steenson and Blake Education 2014
The Islamic architecture of the Moghul period in India  
is a fusion of Arab, Central Asian, Persian and Hindu  
elements. The best known example is the Taj Mahal  
which was completed in 1648.
1 
Kathryn and Adam were visiting the Taj Mahal.  
They were amazed at the symmetry and beauty  
of this building. Adam noticed this tessellation  
in a section of paving. The pattern is formed by  
repeatedly translating a unit design on a square.
a One square is outlined on the diagram. 
Use a coloured pen to outline the grid squares  
on the tessellation.
 
One unit square of the pattern is shown  
in the second diagram.
b How many axes of symmetry are there  
in the unit square?   
 An axis of symmetry is a line where the figure  
can be folded or reflected so that the two halves  
match exactly.
 Draw the axes of symmetry on the diagram. 
c What is the order of rotational symmetry  
of the unit square? 
A figure has rotational symmetry if it exactly  
matches its original position more than once  
when it is turned through one revolution.
2 
At another mausoleum near Agra they found a tiling pattern based on this tessellation.  
It is also formed by repeatedly translating a square unit.
a One square is outlined on the diagram.
 Use a coloured pen to outline the grid squares on the tessellation.
Islamic design 
9

© Paul Steenson and Blake Education 2014

21
 
One unit square of the pattern is shown in this diagram.
b How many axes of symmetry are there?  
Draw the axes of symmetry on the diagram. 
c What is the order of rotational symmetry?
3 
Kathryn and Adam later visited the tomb of the Moghul Emperor Akbar.  
Here they saw a tessellation based on a hexagon.  
Part of the hexagon grid is outlined on the diagram.
a How many axes of symmetry does a regular hexagon (with no design) have?
b What is the order of rotational symmetry of a regular hexagon?
One unit hexagon of the pattern is shown in this diagram.

d What is the order of rotational symmetry?

Maths in the Asia Pacific 
© Paul Steenson and Blake Education 2014
The city of Angkor was the capital of the Khmer 
Empire. Its ruins are located near the modern 
city of Siem Reap in Cambodia.
The temples of Angkor were built during the 
period 802 to 1432. During this time, the 
Khmer Empire was one of the great powers 
of South East Asia. At the height of its power, 
the Khmer Empire ruled over a vast territory 
covering large parts of modern-day Cambodia, 
Laos, Thailand, Myanmar (Burma) and 
southern Vietnam.
Angkor Wat (meaning City Temple) is the 
best known of the temples in this area. It was 
built as a Hindu temple during the reign of 
Suryavarman II (1112 to 1152). It was later 
restored for use as a Buddhist shrine in the  
16th century.
Angkor Wat is surrounded by a moat, 190 metres wide, that forms  
a giant rectangle measuring 1.5 km by 1.3 km. The rectangular wall  
around the enclosure measures 1025 m by 800 m, and has a gate in each side. 
1 
Calculate the perimeter of the moat. 
2 
Calculate the perimeter of the walled enclosure inside the moat. 
3 
What is the area of the enclosure? 
4 
a Calculate the area of the large rectangle, including the moat, in square kilometres.
b Convert your answer to square metres. 
5 
What are the dimensions of the area inside the moat? 
6 
Calculate the area of the moat.
Temples of Angkor

The main entrance to Angkor Wat is on the western side. An avenue 475 m long and  
9.5 m wide leads from the main entrance to the central temple. The central temple complex 
consists of three storeys. The corners of the second and third storeys are marked by towers.  
The central tower rises 31 m above the third storey and 55 m above the ground. 
7 
What is the area of the avenue from the main entrance to the central temple?
8 
How high above the ground is the third storey? 
There are more than 100 temples in the area around Angkor. Many of the temples were left to 
the jungle for centuries and today are found in various stages of decay. 
9 
Banteay Kdai is a massive temple built in the 12th century. It is surrounded by four 
concentric walls. The outer wall measures 700 metres × 500 metres.
a What is the perimeter of the outer wall? 
b Calculate the area enclosed by the outer wall. 
10 Near Banteay Kdai is a large pool, the Pool of Ablutions (Sras Srang). This rectangular 
pool is 400 metres wide. It covers an area of 320 000 square metres.
 
How long is the pool? 
11 Another temple is Preah Khan (Sacred Sword). The temple is surrounded by a wall.  
The area inside the wall is 56 hectares. One side of the rectangle is 800 metres long. 
a Convert 56 hectares to square metres. Hint: 1 hectare = 10 000 square metres.
b How long is the other side of the wall? 
 
12 The fortified city of Angkor Thom was  
enclosed by a square wall 8 metres high  
and 12 kilometres in length. 
 
This was encircled by a moat 100 metres wide.
a What was the length of the wall on one side  
of the city?
b What was the length of one side of the moat?
c What was the area of the city inside the wall?
d What was the area of the city and the moat?
e What was the area of the moat?

24 
Maths in the Asia Pacific 
© Paul Steenson and Blake Education 2014
The Great Wall in northern China is one of the 
great human-made wonders of the world. Like 
a gigantic dragon, the Great Wall winds up and 
down across deserts, grasslands and mountains. 
The first sections were constructed more than 
2 000 years ago by independent kingdoms to 
keep out marauding nomads. These sections 
were later rebuilt and joined together. 
The wall as it is known today dates from the 
Ming Dynasty (1368–1644) when a determined 
effort was made to revitalise the whole project. 
This time, the wall was faced with some 60 
million cubic metres of bricks and stone slabs. 
The Great Wall stretched approximately 
8 850 kilometres from east to west. 
Unfortunately, some of the sections are  
now in ruins or have disappeared.
A comprehensive archaeological survey has concluded that the wall of the Ming era  
measured 8 850 km. This is made up of 6 259 km of actual wall, 359 km of trenches  
and 2 232 km of natural defensive barriers such as hills and rivers.
1 
What percentage, correct to 1 decimal place, of the Ming-era wall was
a actual wall?
b trenches?
c natural defensive barriers?
2 
The average height of the Ming-era Great Wall measured  
10.1 metres and the average width was about 4.6 metres.  
Assume the wall was a rectangular prism.  
Use these dimensions to calculate
a the area of a one face of the wall 1 000 metres long.
b the volume of a 1 kilometre section of the wall.  
Answer in cubic metres.
3 
In the Ming era, the wall was faced with approximately  
60 million cubic metres of bricks and stone slabs.  
The length of actual wall was 6 259 kilometres. 
 
What was the average volume of bricks and stone slabs  
used for each kilometre of the wall?  
Answer to the nearest cubic metre.
The Great Wall of China 
11
ISBN   978 1 92571 065 6

© Paul Steenson and Blake Education 2014 
Maths in the Asia Pacific 
25
One of the best-preserved sections of the Great Wall is situated at Badaling, about  
70 kilometres north of Beijing. Most tourists visit this section of the wall.
Made of stone and bricks from the hills, this portion of the Great Wall is 7.8 metres high and  
5 metres wide. The inside has been formed by tamping earth and small stones, which makes 
the wall very firm and strong. 
4 
Use these dimensions to calculate
a the area of a one face of the wall 500 metres long. 
 
b the volume of a 1 kilometre section of the wall (assuming it is a rectangular prism). 
Give your answer in cubic metres.
The Great Wall of China (cont’d) 
11
6.5 m
6 m
5 m
One of the most striking sections of the Ming Great 
Wall is where it climbs extremely steep slopes.  
In one section, the cross-section is a trapezium.  
The wall has an average height of 6.5 metres.  
It is 6 metres across the bottom, narrowing to  
5 metres across the top.
5 
a Calculate the area of a trapezium 6.5 m high with parallel sides measuring  
5 m and 6 m.
b Calculate the volume of a trapezoidal prism 10 m long, 6.5 m high  
with parallel sides measuring 5 m and 6 m.
c Calculate the volume of a 5 kilometre section of this part of the Great Wall. 
Give your answer in cubic metres. 
Over time, the Great Wall has slowly decayed due to the forces 
of nature. People have removed some of the stone to use in other 
structures. Today, less than 30% of the Great Wall still stands in 
good condition.
6 
What length is 30% of 8 850 km?  
Give your answer correct to the nearest kilometre.

Maths in the Asia Pacific 
© Paul Steenson and Blake Education 2014
Australia has three time zones (ignoring daylight saving in summer):
• 
 Eastern Standard Time is used in Queensland, New South Wales (excluding Broken Hill), 
Victoria, Tasmania and the ACT.
• 
 Central Standard Time is used in South Australia, the Northern Territory and Broken Hill.
• 
 Western Standard Time is used in Western Australia.
Eastern Standard Time is 30 minutes ahead of Central Standard Time.  
It is 30 minutes earlier in Adelaide than Brisbane. 
Eastern Standard Time is 2 hours ahead of Western Standard Time.  
It is 2 hours earlier in Perth than Brisbane.
Papua New Guinea is also in this time zone. 
1 
When it is 8:00 am in Sydney, what is the time in 
a Brisbane? 
b Adelaide? 
c Perth? 
d  Port Moresby (Papua New Guinea)?
2 
When it is 4:30 pm in Mount Hagan (Papua New Guinea), what is the time in 
a Sydney? 
b Darwin?
 
Central Standard Time is 30 minutes behind Eastern Standard Time.  
It is 30 minutes later in Melbourne than Adelaide.  
Central Standard Time is 1 hour and 30 minutes ahead of Western Standard Time.  
It is 1 hour and 30 minutes earlier in Perth than Adelaide.
Japan, Korea and the eastern part of Indonesia are also in this time zone.
3 
When it is 12 noon in Adelaide, what is the time in 
a Melbourne? 
b Perth? 
c Tokyo (Japan)? 
d Seoul (South Korea)?
4 
When it is 1:30 pm in Osaka (Japan), what is the time in 
a Adelaide? 
b Hobart? 
Western Standard Time is 2 hours behind Eastern Standard Time.  
It is 2 hours later in Sydney than Perth. 
Western Standard Time is 1 hour and 30 minutes behind Central Standard Time.  
It is 1 hour and 30 minutes later in Adelaide than Perth.
China, Malaysia and the Philippines are also is this time zone.
5 
When it is 3:00 pm in Perth, what is the time in 
a Brisbane? 
b Adelaide?
c Beijing (China)?  
d Manilla (Philippines)?
Australian time zones & Asian countries 
12
ISBN   978 1 92571 065 6

© Paul Steenson and Blake Education 2014 
Maths in the Asia Pacific 
27
6 
When it is 11:30 am in Kuala Lumpur (Malaysia), what is the time in 
a Perth? 
b Sydney?
7 
Julie was holidaying in Japan.  
At 8:30 am she phoned her family in Adelaide.  
What was the time in Adelaide when Julie phoned? 
8 
Lei called his family in China when  
the time was 10:00 pm in Sydney.  
What was the time in China when he called?
9 
At what time should I make an  
international telephone call from  
Melbourne in order to call
a Japan at 10:00 am?
b China at 6:00 pm?
The following questions use 24-hour time.
24-hour times are used on many airline schedules.
24-hour time starts from midnight (00:00 hours).  
All times are written using 4 digits.  
The first two digits indicate the number of hours after midnight.  
The last two digits indicate the number of minutes.
For example, 14:30 is equal to 2:30 pm.
10 When it is 14:30 in Melbourne, what is the time in 
a Brisbane? 
b Port Moresby (Papua New Guinea)?
11 When it is 11:15 in Perth, what is the time in 
a Adelaide? 
b Beijing (China)?
12 When it is 21:40 in Adelaide, what is the time in
a Sydney? 
b Tokyo (Japan)?
13 A plane leaves Brisbane at 14:20.  
It takes 3 hours 5 minutes to fly from Brisbane to Port Moresby (Papua New Guinea). 
What is the local time when this plane arrives in Port Moresby? 
14 A plane leaves Perth at 07:50.  
It takes 5 hours 40 minutes to fly from Perth to Kuala Lumpur (Malaysia).  
What is the local time when this plane arrives in Kuala Lumpur? 
15 A plane leaves Beijing (China) at 08:40.  
It takes 13 hours to fly from Beijing to Sydney.  
What is the local time when this plane arrives in Sydney?
16 Natalie caught a plane from Kuala Lumpur (Malaysia) to Adelaide.  
The flight took 7 hours and 20 minutes, non-stop.  
The plane left Kuala Lumpur at 23:55.  
At what time did the plane arrive in Adelaide?

Australia has three time zones (ignoring daylight saving in summer):
• 
 Eastern Standard Time is used in Queensland, New South Wales (excluding Broken Hill),

The following questions use 24-hour time.

All times are written using 4 digits.  
The first two digits indicate the number of hours after midnight.  
The last two digits indicate the number of minutes.
For example, 16:20 is equal to 4:20 pm.

What is the local time when this plane arrives in Sydney?

What is the local time when this plane arrives in Melbourne?

The flight left Brisbane at 08:20 and is due to arrive in Auckland at 14:35.  
How long is Casey’s flight?

As natural forests have been logged for timber or cleared for farming, efforts have been  
made to plant new forests. In most countries, the proportion of planted forest remained  
low in 2010. However, in Thailand and Vietnam planted forests make up a significant  
proportion of the total forest area.

area

Through the centuries the Chinese used characters for writing numbers.  
They were very advanced in their mathematics and it is believed that they had a  
highly developed number system as early as 1 500 bc.
There are characters representing the numbers 1 to 10.  
Other characters are used for larger numbers like 100 and 1 000.
The basic symbols are:
Writing numbers using the Chinese characters is similar to writing out numbers in  
English (e.g. ‘one thousand, nine hundred, forty-five’). Since it reflects spoken language,  
the Chinese system does not use the positional system we use with Hindu-Arabic numerals.
Multiples of 10, 100 and 1 000 are constructed using a multiplication principle.  
For example, 30 is written vertically, using the symbols for 3 and 10 as 3 times 10:

The abacus was one of the earliest calculating machines developed.  
It is used by pushing beads up or down.  
The diagram shows a type of abacus used in Japan.
The value of the bead is determined by the column it lies in.  
The place values work right to left. The far right column of beads is the units column.  
Moving to the left, we have the tens column then the hundreds column and then the 
thousands column.
Above the beam the corresponding values of the heaven beads, right to left,

Food safety is the focus of celebrity chefs Ada and Lorenzo’s latest episode. They venture into the 
world of the bugs that multiply in our food if we don’t watch out. They know that food safety in the 
kitchen will stop them from getting sick. 
Where you see an ‘idea’ provided for a question, complete the calculations in it to find the answer.
1 
a How many cases of food poisoning occur every year in Australia? 
 
 Idea: 3 × 5 × 7 × 9 
189
 million
b If 1 in 5 cases of food poisoning is caused by incorrect  
food handling in the home, how many cases is this?
2 
In the right conditions, how long does it take a single  
food-poisoning bacterium to grow into more than  
two million bacteria? 
 
Idea: 3 × 5 × 7 × 9 
135

3 
Food-poisoning bacteria grow and multiply fastest in the temperature range  
called the ‘danger zone’. What range of temperatures in °C is this danger zone? 
 
Idea: between a and b, where b is 12 times a and the difference between a and b is 55 
4 
What is the longest time you can leave high risk foods like meat, dairy, eggs, seafood, 
prepared foods and processed meats in the danger zone before they are no longer  
safe to eat? 
 
Idea: the time it takes the minute hand of a clock to travel through 720°
5 
At what temperature in degrees Celsius should most food be cooked? 
 
Idea: 25 more than (25 less than double 25) plus 25 
6 
To be called ‘low fat’, milk must contain less than 3% fat. How much fat should there be 
in one litre of low fat milk?
7

original product. If ‘Ratrap’ cheese has 48% fat, how much fat can the ‘Reduced fat 
Ratrap’ cheese contain?
8

then ‘fat free’?
9

a bit of this and a pinch of that!
10 Food additives are used to improve flavour, add colour or preserve. They can cause 
allergies in some people, so they are always listed on the packaging. Some additives used 
are listed in the table on the next page. Refer to it to answer the question below.
a Cochineal is a red colouring that comes from a beetle. What additive number is it?
b MSG is often used in Asian cooking. What additive number is it?
c How many different preservatives are listed?
d If an additive is a two hundred number, what sort of additive is it likely to be?
e How many additives are listed altogether?

A wok is a very useful cooking vessel that appears 
in various cultures in Asia, Japan, India and various 
western countries. It is a wonderful way to stir-fry, can 
work as a deep fryer, a soup pot, a slow cooker and a 
general pan in the kitchen. It can also be used as the 
base for a steamer basket. The steamer shown contains 
two baskets in which to prepare a variety of foods.

•  250 g green 
beans

sliced

takes about 10 minutes.

thickness, not the weight of the roast. 
 
‘When you double the thickness of a roast it takes four times as long to cook through, and 
nine times as long when you treble the thickness,’ Dr Spec said.

temperature used to cook meat in a pan is 160°C.

What is the new cooking time for the steak if it took 9 minutes originally?
b Dr Spec wants her steak medium rare. For this, the cooking time needs to be reduced by 
a further 9%. How long did Dr Spec’s steak take to cook?

meat.
III  Place on a rack in a roasting pan 
and bake in the centre of the oven, 
basting occasionally until meat 
cooks to either rare, medium or 
well done.
IV  Rest for 15 minutes before carving.

Gas Mark 5? How is that going to cook my cheese cake? Is it 350º Fahrenheit (F) or is it 180º 
Celsius (C)? In this episode, TV celebrity chefs Lorenzo and Ada are going to bake an authentic Italian 
cheese cake originating from Lorenzo’s home town of Pescara, on the Adriatic coast.
oven and out!
Around the world, ovens vary in the way they cook. Wood-fired ovens are complicated to use 
and require a lot of experience. Folklore has it that once the oven seemed hot to touch, a small 
fistful of flour would be thrown into the oven to see how long it took to brown, as a guide to 
temperature! Today’s ovens are generally heated by electricity or gas, and have been built to 
accurately control temperature. 
1 
Lorenzo’s Italian cheese cake is to be cooked at 350°F for  
45 minutes. 
a Use the fast oven facts to find the equivalent Celsius 
temperature in a conventional oven.
b What would be the equivalent  
Gas Mark setting?

temperature in a fan-forced electric 
oven if it needed 45 minutes in a 
conventional oven?

time for the cheese cake in  
a fan-forced oven?
... Fast Food FaCts
Gas Mark is the old term for 
the temperature setting on 
an oven.
160°C = 300°F = Gas Mark 3
170°C = 325°F = Gas Mark 4
180°C = 350°F = Gas Mark 5
Fan-forced ovens circulate 
the hot air in the oven and 
so the food cooks 10% faster 
at a 20°C cooler temperature 
than a conventional (not 
fan-forced) oven.
Recipe – Lorenzo’s Cheese Cake – Crostata di Ricotta
Ingredients (serves 12)
•  750 g fresh ricotta 
cheese
•  200 g caster sugar 
•  125 g double cream 
•  4 eggs (60 g each) 
separated
•  30 mL Sambuca 
liquor
•  10 g icing sugar to 
dust  
Pastry base
•  150 g plain flour 
•  60 g almond meal 
•  50 g icing sugar
•  125 g cold butter, 
chopped 
•  1 egg (60 g)
Method
Collecting all the ingredients takes about 15 minutes. 
I 
 Process the flour, almond meal, icing sugar and butter in 
the bowl of a food processor for 2 minutes. Add the egg 
and process for another 1 minute. Knead until smooth on a 
floured board (5 minutes). Shape into a disc and cover with a 
tea towel. Place in the refrigerator for 30 minutes.
II 
 Preheat oven to 350ºF for 20 minutes. Roll out the pastry to 
a 3 mm thick disc. Line a tin with pastry. The tin should be 
round with a removable base and base radius measurement of 
20 cm. Be tidy. 
III  Cover the pastry base with baking paper and fill with pastry 
weights, rice or dried beans, to stop it rising. Place on a baking 
tray and bake in the oven for 10 minutes. Remove the paper 
and weights and bake for a further 10 minutes or until golden. 
IV  Separate eggs. Beat the yolks, ½ of the caster sugar, ricotta 
cheese and Sambuca. Add the cream and set aside.
V 
 Whip eggs whites until stiff, for about 4 minutes, and then 
add the other half of the caster sugar. Combine with the 
cheese mixture and place it into the tin that has the pastry 
and bake for 45 minutes at 350ºF. Cool for 1 hour then dust 
with the 10 g of icing sugar. Serve.

In this episode, TV celebrity chefs Lorenzo and Ada investigate the equipment used by chefs to 
turn out the dishes they prepare. They must get out their tape measures and find the right kitchen 
equipment for cooking. Mathematical capability in the kitchen is important for success. 
1 
Will a roast turkey measuring 360 mm by 280 mm by 240 mm fit in my microwave oven 
which has the dimensions width 31.5 cm, height 26 cm and depth 29.4 cm? 
2 
A piece of kitchen paper 20 cm square is to be used to line the bottom of a cake tin to stop 
the cake sticking to it. The folding is done as shown. You can try it yourself!
a Approximately what shape will the paper be when you cut it as shown?
b Will the shape fit snugly in the bottom of a pan of radius 10 cm?
3 
A microwave oven is advertised as having a capacity of 27 L with the interior dimensions 
width 359 mm, height 217 mm and depth 352 mm, and with the exterior dimensions 
width 510 mm, height 304 mm and depth 380 mm. 
a Find the interior capacity (volume) of the microwave oven in litres, correct to 2 decimal 
places. Hint: 1 cm3  1 mL
b Is the advertised capacity correct?
c Find the exterior capacity of the microwave oven.
4 
A wall oven has a capacity of 59 L. The oven is 46 cm wide and 42 cm deep inside. How 
high is the inside of the oven in centimetres, correct to 2 decimal places?
5 
A free-standing stove is 895 mm wide and 600 mm deep. How high is it if the outside 
volume is 92 000 cubic centimetres?
6 
The turntable inside a microwave oven has a 
diameter of 300 mm. What is the area of the

An electric oven measures 46 cm wide, 28 cm high and 42 cm deep inside. There are two 
racks that can be placed in any of the 5 equally spaced positions. The lowest position of 
the rack is on the bottom and the highest position is 3 cm below the top.
a What is the largest possible gap between the two racks?
b What is the smallest possible gap between the two racks?  
Hint: think how many spaces there will be between  
the 5 positions.
8 
a Find the length of the diagonal across the base of a  
rectangular baking dish measuring 24 cm by 18 cm.  
Hint: use Pythagoras’ Theorem. 
b What area of an oven rack is not covered by the baking  
dish in part a if the oven rack is 46 cm by 42 cm?

Maths in the Kitchen 
© Barbara Lynch, Angelo Pantalone and Blake Education 2009
Waste or waist? 
11
Celebrity chefs Ada and Lorenzo are shooting the next episode of their TV cooking show at Lorenzo’s 
house. Picture Lorenzo’s refrigerator: a carrot, some cauliflower, 6 beans, some garlic, the last of the 
sliced ham, one egg, half a tin of pineapple and some pretty hard cheese. Using his leftovers will save 
his wasted food from the rubbish tip where it would cause nasty methane gas. 
Where you see an ‘idea’ provided for a question, complete the calculations in it to find the answer.
1 
Using leftovers for one meal allowed Lorenzo to have one 
‘free’ meal every week. If, on average, a meal at home 
costs $8.52, how much does Lorenzo save every year of  
52 weeks by using his leftovers this way?
2 
A worldwide chain of coffee houses has a policy of 
keeping a tap running continuously to keep their utensils 
clean. As a result, they waste 23 million litres of water per 
day. How many billions (thousand millions) of litres of 
water do they waste in a year of 365 days?
3 
5 percent of a particular country’s leftovers would feed the 
4 million people of Costa Rica for a whole day. Botswana 
has a population of 1.6 million. What percentage of 
leftovers from this particular country would feed the 
people of Botswana for a day?
4 
In 2004, the approximately 20 400 000 Australians put three million tonnes or  
$5 billion worth of food in the rubbish bin. A billion is a thousand million.
a What mass in whole number kilograms per year is that per person? 
b What value of food in dollars and cents per year is that per person? 
c Correct to 1 decimal place, what mass in kilograms is that per person?
d Correct to 1 decimal place, what value of food in dollars and cents per week is that per 
person?
e Each week in Australia, the equivalent of one in five supermarket bags full of food goes 
in the rubbish and hence into landfill. If each full supermarket bag weighs 3 kg, find for 
each Australian, each year, the number of supermarket bags full of food: 
 i trashed 
       ii purchased. 
5 
It has been noted that nearly half of all food 
bought by American households is wasted. 
a If the average American household wastes  
$US 500 per year in uneaten food, how much 
does that household spend on food each year?
b If there are 115 million households in the  
United States, find the total amount spent on:
 i uneaten food     
 ii food altogether.
... Fast LEFtovER FaCts
   Don’t buy too much.
   Don’t ‘buy one get one free’ 
unless you need two.
   Don’t shop hungry.
   Plan meals and buy only for 
them.
   Only buy frozen food in 
bulk.
   Organise your fridge.
   You can cook once and eat 
twice by cooking double, 
but remember to reheat at a 
high enough temperature.
ISBN  978 1 92571 015 1

© Barbara Lynch, Angelo Pantalone and Blake Education 2009 
Maths in the Kitchen

Waste or waist? (cont’d) 
11
6 
On average, households in Britain throw away a third of all food they buy and half of 
that is edible. If these households waste between £UK250 and £UK400 of edible food each 
year, how much do households spend on food each year?
7 
The amount of food wasted by the average person in Britain each year is UK£350 worth. 
If this amounts to 408.7 million tonnes being dumped by the 61 million people in Britain, 
find:
a what weight of food in kilograms is dumped by each person in Britain
b the amount of money wasted in dumped food in Britain.
dumped food waste produces methane gas! 
8 
What weight in millions of tonnes of the world’s 
methane emissions are produced each year by  
food dumped as landfill? 
 
Idea: between a and b, where a is the even  
number between 29 and 31, and b is 10 times  
the prime number between 5 and 11. Remember,  
a prime number is a number whose only factors  
are itself and one.
9 
According to statistics taken in Japan, companies who manufacture and sell food, 
together with the restaurants that prepare food, produce 11 million tonnes of food waste 
each year. Also, 70% of food leftovers are recycled, half being turned into animal feed. 
a How much food waste in whole number tonnes is recycled:
 i altogether?  
 ii into animal feed?
b This means that less than 5% of the food waste is turned into the greenhouse gas, 
methane. How much methane in tonnes is produced?
10 Methane gas can be used to produce clean electricity.  
One million tonnes of waste dumped as landfill at 
Cranville produced 4 million cubic metres (m3) of landfill 
gas within a year of the tip being closed. Half of the gas 
was methane. 
a What volume of methane was produced by a  
million tonnes of waste?
b 1 Watt hour (Wh) is the power of 1 Watt used for  
1 hour. An electric stove uses 8 thousand Watts  
(8 kilowatts or 8 kW) hours. How many kilowatts  
will the stove use if it is on for 3 hours?
c Power is sold by the kilowatt hour. If a megawatt hour 
(MWh) is a million Watt hours, how many kWh are 
there in a MWh?
d The methane gas from Cranville tip can produce  
5000 MWh of electricity and this can be sold at 7 cents 
per kWh. How much can be earned from selling the  
gas from Cranville as electricity?
... Fast Food WastE FaCts
•  Producing food produces a fifth of 
carbon emissions.
•  Decomposing food releases methane.
•  Most landfill methane currently 
comes from developed countries.
•  Developed countries make more 
waste.

Maths in the Kitchen 
© Barbara Lynch, Angelo Pantalone and Blake Education 2009
In this episode Lorenzo and Ada go on safari to discover how food ends up on our plates! It is 
important to understand the process involved in food production and handling; for instance, how 
seasonality and freshness contribute to nutritional value. Do you know how chicken is reared to 
become delicious roast chicken? 
Processing
The processors own the new-born chicks and transport them to farmers for rearing. Once the 
chickens are the right weight, the processors sell them to the retailer. 
1 
Use the fast processing facts to answer the following questions.
a The processor is rearing 100 000 organically-fed chicks to produce premium meat. 
When the chicken weighs 2.5 kilograms it is sold to a retailer. How much has the 
processor spent in feed on rearing the chickens?
b The processor on-sells to the retailer for $3.75 per kilogram of chicken meat. How much 
income should the processor expect?
on the farm – farmers rear chickens for the processors
2 
Use the fast farm facts to answer the following 
questions.
a Given that the usual price paid per chicken by 
the processor is 65 cents, how much income 
should the farmer expect from selling the entire 
flock of 100 000 chickens?
b If each chicken yields 1.75 kilograms of meat, 
how much chicken meat in kilograms has the 
farmer grown?
c If the farmer gets 37.1 cents per kilogram of 
chicken meat, how much will the farmer make 
from the flock of chickens?
d If the return on investment – that is, the profit – is 8.7 cents per chicken,  
how much has the farmer made on the entire flock?
e The associated cost to farm the chickens has been 91.3% of money paid  
by the processor. How much money is that?
In the shops!
3 
Use the fast retail facts to answer the following question. 
 
A specialty retailer who sells organic produce purchases  
the entire flock for re-sale. How much retail income does  
100 000 units at $6.50 per kilogram represent? 
Paddock to plate! 
12
... Fast FaRM FaCts
•  Generally a farmer is paid  
65 cents per chicken produced 
by the processor. A typical bird 
weighs about 2.5 kilograms.
•  Each chicken produces about 
1.75 kilograms of meat.
•  The farmer usually gets  
37.1 cents per kilogram of 
chicken meat.
•  Return on investment (ROI) per 
bird is 8.7 cents per chicken.
... Fast REtaIL FaCts
Usually retailers sell whole 
chickens for approximately 
$6.50 per kilogram.
... Fast PRoCEssING FaCts
•  It costs chicken processors 
approximately $1.40 in feed to 
produce 1 kilogram of chicken.
•  Chicken processors on-sell  
chickens to retailers for 
approximately $3.75 per kilogram.

Most growers keep apples fresh by storing them in a controlled 
atmosphere (CA) room where the temperature is 32° Fahrenheit 
and oxygen is replaced with nitrogen to slow ripening. 
4 
What is 32° Fahrenheit in Celsius? Use the formula: 
 
°C = (5 
9)(°F – 32)

harvested. How many kilograms of fruit could that yield?
b If each apple weighs approximately 150 grams, how many 
apples would that be?
c How many kilojoules are there in the average apple?
d How much of the total yield of apples by weight is water?
How do you like them apples!
The American White House is hosting a dinner for 850 guests.  
The head chef is baking American apple pies using Australian apples! 
The apples will be air-freighted from Melbourne to Washington.
6 
Use the fast food facts to answer the following questions.
a How many apples are there in each box?
b What is the weight of the apples in a palette?
c How many apples are there in each palette?
d 108 boxes of apples are going to the USA. Find:
 i the number of palettes that will be needed
 ii the weight of the apples in kilograms
 iii the total number of apples in the consignment.
e The apple pie recipe indicates that 2 kg of apples are required to make a delicious pie. 
How many pies will our consignment of apples make?
Who’s forking the bill?
The air-freight charge includes pick-up, freight, handling, fuel surcharge, documentation fee, 
security, insurance, delivery to destination and GST, and is $5.25 per kg.
7 
Each box of apples costs AUD$64.00 to grow and harvest. Use your answers to Question 6 
to answer the following questions.

be mature and in 
full production after 
approximately 9 years.

approximately  
150 kilograms of fruit.

and 0% fat.

kilojoule, nutritious food 
at 220 kJ per 100 grams.

weighs 150 grams. 
... Fast Food FaCts

Melbourne to Washington:
•  Each box contains 16 kg of 
apples at 160 grams per apple.

a What is the cost per kg of the apples to 
grow and harvest?
b What is the cost of each apple to grow 
and harvest, assuming that the weight 
of an apple averages 150 grams?
c What is the total cost of growing 
and harvesting all the apples in the 
consignment?
d What is the total air-freight charge for 
the 4 palettes?
e What is the total cost of the apples for 
the White House dinner?
f What is the total cost of the apples  
per kg?
g What is the total cost of the apples  
per pie?

In their latest episode, TV celebrity chefs Ada and Lorenzo are going green! Organic foods are foods 
grown according to certain standards, without unnatural pesticides, fertilisers or sewage sludge and 
processed without food additives. Generally they are not genetically modified (GM). Types of organic 
produce available include fruit and vegetables, grains, meat and meat products, honey and some 
processed foods.
Pick me or not?
1

a further $65 million per year was received through exports. What was the combined 
domestic and export value of organic food in 2008?
b Consumer demand led to an increase in domestic 
sales of 12.5% in 2009. What would the Australian 
organic market be worth in 2009?
c If Australian organic food represented 1.5% of global 
organic food sales in 2008, what would be the global 
figure, rounded to the nearest billion? 
2

food produced in Australia is expected to be about 30% 
annually. Use your answer to question 1a to find the 
total dollar value you would expect it to be worth in:
a 2009?  
b 2010? 
c 2011?  
d 2012?

organic fruits and vegetables on his 150 acre farm.

rear jersey cows. Gwen needs 10 acres to feed 50 cows.  
How many cows can Gwen feed?

c Each of Gwen’s milk-producing cows is milked twice a 
day and yields 1.5 litres of milk per session. The cows are 
milked 52 weeks of the year. How much milk do Gwen’s 
cows produce each year?
d Non-organic milk is sold at $0.40 a litre, but Gwen’s milk 
is sold at 15% more per litre. How much money will Gwen 
make from selling milk each year?
Climate change and organic food production 
5 
There is a drought in Far North Queensland which has affected the price of bananas. 
They were $5.99 per kg before the drought, but the price has increased by 37%. What is 
the new price?
the nature of organics!

tracing minerals?

Chilli Pepper Contest
The heat in chillies is often measured in Scoville units. These units are named after Wilbur 
Scoville who, in 1912, used tasters to tell him how much sugar and water was needed to get rid 
of the heat of a particular chilli. Today, scientific methods are used to measure the capsaicin 
which causes the heat in chillies.

On their previous episode, TV celebrity chefs Ada and Lorenzo featured a Chilli Pepper Contest and a Soup

taRP? are we talking tents?

Bottled, spotted and spinners - dolphins 
1
Dolphins live in the oceans and are closely related to whales and porpoises. There are almost  
40 species of dolphin. They are found worldwide, mostly in the shallower seas of the continental 
shelves. Dolphins are carnivores, and eat mostly fish and squid. They are considered to be among the 
most intelligent of animals, and their often friendly appearance and seemingly playful attitude 
have made them popular with humans.
1

a carnivore 
b breach 
c sloughed 
d conical
2 
Bottlenose Dolphins are on average 3.6 m long, weigh 500 kg and live for 45 years. An 
average human is 1.72 m high, 75 kg and lives for 80 years. Draw three column graphs 
to compare the average dolphin with the average human. Think carefully about the 
horizontal and vertical scales in your graphs.

In each of these pods, how many dolphins would you expect to live to the maximum age?
a 150 dolphins

c 250 dolphins
d 600 dolphins 
e 470 dolphins

13 The smooth skin of a dolphin reduces its drag in the water and thus increases its 
swimming speed. The skin is kept smooth by constantly being sloughed off and replaced. 
A Bottlenose Dolphin replaces its outermost layer of skin every two hours. This is nine 
times the rate of human skin renewal. Calculate the number of times a dolphin sheds its 
outermost layer of skin during each time listed.

6 
Maths in the Wild 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
Fish ‘n’ chips – sharks 
2
Sharks are a type of fish with a full cartilaginous skeleton and a streamlined body. They breathe 
with the use of five to seven gill slits. Sharks have a covering of dermal denticles (the skin feels like 
sandpaper) to protect their skin from damage and from parasites and to improve fluid dynamics. 
They also have replaceable teeth.
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a cartilaginous 
b dermal 
c denticle 
d embryos  
e predatory
Sharks range in size from the small Spined Pygmy Shark, a deep sea species of only  
22 centimetres in length, to the Whale Shark, the largest fish, which grows to a length of 
approximately 12 metres and 25 tonnes. The White Pointer grows to 7 m and 2 tonnes,  
Tiger Sharks to 5 m and 900 kg, Thresher Sharks to 5 m and 0.4 tonnes and Basking Sharks  
to 12.3 m and 19 tonnes. Humans can be up to 272 cm tall and 310 kg in weight.
2 
Draw column graphs to compare the height and weight of a human with those of the 
given sharks.
 
Height  
 
 
 
 
 
       Weight
The teeth of carnivorous sharks are not attached to the jaw, but embedded in the flesh. In 
many species, the teeth are constantly replaced throughout the shark’s life. Sharks have about 
3 000 teeth spread over 5 rows. The front set is the largest and does most of the work. In some 
sharks, a row of teeth is replaced every two weeks. Sharks live for approximately 25 years.
3 
a Approximately how many teeth does a shark have in a single row?
b How many teeth are replaced every four weeks?
4 
Calculate the approximate number of teeth each 
shark may have in its lifetime, if it lives for:
a 5 years. 
b 12 years.
c 2 years. 
d 15 years.
e 25 years.
Sharks rarely attack humans unless provoked. In 
2006, there were approximately 98 shark attacks on 
humans. Of these attacks, 64 were unprovoked and 
18 were provoked, with the remainder uncertain. 
5 
Calculate the approximate percentage of  
attacks that were:
a provoked. 
b unprovoked.

Great Whites account for about five-twelfths of all annual reported shark attacks. Of these 
Great White attacks, about one-third of the people die.
a If 100 shark attacks were reported in one year, how many would be Great White attacks?
b How many people would die from this number of Great White attacks? 
Great White Sharks are ovoviviparous – that is, the eggs are kept inside the female body until 
they hatch. About 40 eggs develop in the female’s uterus, hatching there and continuing to 
develop until they are born. The Great White has an 11 month gestation (pregnancy) period. 
There is not much room for the embryos to grow and they must eat each other to make more 
room – these sharks develop their predatory skills well before they enter the wild. On average, 
8 Great White Sharks are born from an original litter of 40. Great White Sharks reach sexual 
maturity at about 12 years and live for 40 to 100 years.
9 
What is the probability of a Great White being born?
10 Assuming the shark can get pregnant again straight after she gives birth, how many 
sharks could be born to a Great White female that died at the age of:
a 50 years? 
b 100 years?
11 Sharks are popular for their flesh – the ‘flake’ in ‘fish-n-chips’ is shark. About 2 190 tonnes 
of shark is landed from the Southern Shark Fishery each year. This makes the annual 
wholesale value of the fishery AU$13.831 million. Each shark caught weighs about 15 kg. 
a How many sharks are caught per year in the Southern Park Fishery?
b What is the approximate wholesale monetary value of one of these sharks?

8 
Maths in the Wild 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
Whales are mammals and are more closely related to humans than to the many fish and creatures 
they share the oceans with. Like us, they are warm-blooded, give birth to live young and suckle 
their young. Baleen Whales are characterised by having baleen plates for filtering food from water, 
rather than teeth. This distinguishes them from the other group of whales, the toothed whales or 
Odontoceti.
Whenever you see a colour code letter, find your answer in the shape at the end of the 
worksheet and colour that section. Colour code: R = red, B = blue, G = green, Y = yellow. 
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a weaning 
b lunge  
c  breach
2 
Whales are the largest living animals on Earth. The 
average length and weight of some species are shown 
in the table. In your workbook, draw column graphs 
to compare the length and weight of these whales with 
that of an elephant and an orca. Draw one graph for 
length and a second graph for weight.
Commercial whaling in Australia started in about 1820.  
By 1845, twenty-six thousand Southern Right Whales  
had been killed. Almost 100 years later, they were a 
protected species. Between 1936 and 1938, approximately 
twelve thousand Humpback Whales were killed. A 10 year 
moratorium on Humpback whaling was declared in 1939. 
After killing commenced again in 1949, almost sixteen 
thousand Humpbacks were killed in Australia by 1963. 
Australia ceased whaling in 1978.
3 
Calculate the average number of whales killed per year in Australia between:
a 1820 and 1845. (R) 
b 1936 and 1938. (B) 
c 1949 and 1963. (G)
4 
Suggest an explanation for the large increase in your average answer to question 3b 
compared to 3a.
5 
During the whaling operations, it was found that approximately 1 200 whales provided 
eleven thousand tonnes of oil.

another saw 500. What was the average number of whales observed? (Y)

figure of 2000. (Y)

Octopus, squid and cuttlefish live in the oceans and do not have backbones. They are Cephalopoda, 
which means ‘head foot’. Members of this group have feet or tentacles connected to the head, 
not the body. They can change the colour of their skin to mimic their environment and hide from 
predators. They also eject a thick blackish ink in a large cloud to help them escape from predators. 
They can move quickly by sucking water into their mantle cavity and quickly squirting it out of 
their siphon in a fast, strong jet.
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a lair 
b larval 
c respiratory 
d  chameleon.
Octopuses have 8 arms which create an umbrella  
shape around their central rounded head. Each  
arm has two rows of suckers and is 3 to 4 times longer  
than the body. The head has two large eyes. Octopuses  
can be many different colours, from red to a pale grey, with or  
without mottling and with or without protrusions on their skin.
2

a 5                 b  7                  c  25               d  53                  e  49
3 
How many octopuses are there for these numbers of arms?
a 16               b  24                 c  104             d  216                e  560
In some species of octopus, the female lays 200 000 eggs. She hangs these  
eggs in strings from the ceiling of her lair. At around the time the eggs hatch,  
the mother dies and the young larval octopuses spend a period of time drifting in  
clouds of plankton where they feed.
4

b 7 
c 9

When Blue Ringed Octopus mate in early autumn, the male dies. The female lays 
approximately 50 eggs in late autumn. Once the eggs are hatched 6 months later, the female 
dies. The young octopuses develop quickly, and mature and mate the following autumn.
8

Within 10 seconds, the victim is blind. Within one minute, there is a loss of sense of touch,

arrest within a further 3 minutes. Draw a timeline to show the effects of the octopus bite.

‘under twenty-five’ and refers to the number of octopuses per kilogram – in this case, 
fewer than twenty-five octopuses per kilogram. 26!!40 is pronounced ‘twenty-six forty’ and

Flowers of the sea - anemones and jellyfish 
5
Sea anemones are a group of water-dwelling, predatory animals. They are named after the 
anemone, a flower found in many gardens. Sea anemones are closely related to coral and jellyfish. 
A jellyfish has no head, brain, heart, eyes or ears. It has no bones, either. To capture prey for food, 
jellyfish have a net of tentacles that contains poisonous, stinging cells. When the tentacles brush 
against prey – or a person’s leg – thousands of tiny stinging cells explode, launching barbed stingers 
and poison into the victim. 
Whenever you see a colour code letter, find your answer in the shape at the end of the 
worksheet and colour that section. Colour code: R = red, B = blue, G = green, Y = yellow.

Measuring up to 20 cm along each side of its cube or bell, the

on each one.

the victim develops a severe backache or headache, and shooting

Jellyfish feed on the same kinds of prey as fish. If fish are removed from an environment, 
jellyfish are likely to move in. Depleted fish stocks have decreased competition for jellyfish, 
allowing them to breed to plague proportions. Japan has experienced plagues of the giant 
jellyfish Nomura, which can grow to more than a metre wide and weigh up to 150 kg. 
These jellyfish cause major problems if they become caught in fishing gear, boat engines or 
mechanical equipment. Fishers have reported cases of more than 800 of these jellyfish being 
caught in a single net.

Marinara on the menu  – oysters and scallops 
6
Bivalves are molluscs. They have two-part shells. This group of animals includes scallops, clams, 
oysters and mussels. Bivalves are exclusively aquatic and are found in marine and fresh water. 
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a salinity 
b hessian
The oyster becomes sexually mature at about 1 year of age, and then always as a male. After 
about 3 years, it can change sex and reproduce as a female. From then on it can change sex 
back and forth throughout its life. When reproduction takes place, the male releases its sperm 
into the water and the female sucks it in to her shell and fertilises the eggs. A female can 
contain as many as 1.1 million eggs. Fertilised eggs develop within the female in the first  
10 days. The larvae swim freely in the water for a couple of weeks and so spread to other 
areas. Afterwards, the larvae fall to the bottom and land on rocks, shells or stakes. Then the 
oyster is known as a brood and it is about 0.3 mm in size. The oyster lives for about 8 years.
2 
Draw a timeline on the line below to show the life cycle of an oyster. Then in your 
workbook draw and annotate a diagram of the life cycle.
3 
If a female fertilises 1.1 million eggs, how many oysters would grow to adulthood for each 
of these survival rates?
a 1% 
b 2% 
c 0.002% 
d 0.003% 
e 0.0001% 
4 
If reproduction is to take place, salinity is important – there must be at least 1 part salt to 
40 parts water. Simplify the salinity of these batches of water, and decide if reproduction 
can take place. 
a 2:20 
b 2:100 
c 5:400 
d 4:120 
e 2:90
Oysters are filter feeders – that is, they consume a variety of species of phytoplankton, bacteria 
and viruses from the surrounding water. Adult oysters can filter 10 L of water per hour as they 
search for food. 
5 
How much water could an oyster filter in: 
a 2 hr? 
b 3 hr?  
c 6.5 hr? 
d 5 hr 30 min? 
e 6 hr 25 min?
6 
How long would it take an oyster to filter: 
a 50 L? 
b 70 L? 
c 65 L? 
d 125 L?  
e 241 L?
The harvesting of oysters in oyster farms for market occurs prior to spawning, when the oysters 
are in peak condition. Oysters are brought in from the farm and graded into various shell 
sizes, such as bistro 50–60 mm, plate 60–70 mm and standard 70–85 mm. The oysters are then 
packed into hessian bags. For bistro oysters, 45 dozen oysters are packaged in each bag. Then 
the oysters are transported in refrigerated trucks directly to the wholesaler or retailer. Oysters 
stored at 5°C have a shelf-life of less than 10 days.
7 
How many hessian bags are needed to store these numbers of bistro oysters?
a 90 dozen 
b 225 dozen 
c 440 dozen 
d 4 860 oysters 
e 24 300 oysters

Scallops are edible bivalves, similar to oysters and clams. They are found on the bottom of 
bay waters and in the sea. They do not attach themselves to a permanent anchorage. Instead, 
they move themselves through the water by opening and closing their shells. As a result, the 
muscle that controls the ‘hinge’ of the shell is much larger than that of oysters or clams. 
Scallops in Bass Strait are collected in dredges which are towed along the seabed by vessels 
travelling at four to six knots. The dredges are made from strong, wire-mesh boxes that are 
four metres long, with a mouth about three metres wide and 30 cm high. 2.5 scallops per 
square metre is considered the minimum economic limit for dredge fishers.

Weedy dragons and wet horses - seahorses 
7
Seahorses belong to the family of fish which also includes pipefish and leafy sea dragons. There are 
over 32 species of seahorse. They are mainly found in tropical and subtropical coastal and reef 
waters all over the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans. All seahorses have bodies that are protected 
by strong external plates, arranged into a series of ‘rings’. These rings help to protect the body of 
the fish, but also result in the fish having only limited flexibility of the body. 
Seahorses stay in small areas. On average, males stay in one square metre of habitat and 
females in one hundred times that area. They bob around in sea grass meadows, mangrove 
stands and coral reefs where they are camouflaged by their murky brown and grey patterns 
which blend into the sea grass backgrounds.
1 
How many male seahorses could be found in each of these habitats?
a  
               b 
 
                    c

Seahorses and pipefishes are notable for being the only species in which males become 
‘pregnant’. The male seahorse can give birth to 2 000 babies at a time. Pregnancies last 
anywhere from 10 to 25 days.
5

Out of every 1000 infants born, fewer than five survive to adulthood, which helps to explain 
why litters are so large. The survival rates of these infants is actually fairly high compared to 
most fish. This is because they are sheltered in their father’s pouch during the earliest stages of 
development. The eggs of most other fish are abandoned immediately after fertilisation.

Seahorse populations have been endangered in recent years by overfishing. In Australia, 
seahorse fishing is strictly illegal. The seahorse is used in traditional Chinese herbology, 
and as many as 20 million seahorses might be caught each year and sold for this purpose. 
Unfortunately, seahorses around the world are rapidly moving towards becoming an 
endangered species. There is a huge trade in seahorses and their underwater habitats are 
threatened by pollution.

a 1 day?

Seahorses lack a tail fin. Since this fin provides most fish with their main swimming power, 
seahorses don’t swim very fast. However, they are extremely maneuverable, and can hover 
precisely. Seahorses can swim forwards or backwards by moving their dorsal and pectoral fins. 
The main thrust comes from their dorsal fin, which beats 70 times a minute. Pectoral fins on 
each side of the face are used to steer.
11 How many times does the dorsal fin beat in:
a 3 minutes? 
b 5 minutes? 
c 10 seconds? 
d 3 hours? 
e 1.2 hours?

a 490 beats in 5 minutes 
b 210 beats in 3 minutes

e 2 beats in 0.8 seconds

each day. Seahorses have no teeth and swallow  
their food whole.

18 
Maths in the Wild 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
Exciting echinoderms - starfish 
8
Starfish or sea stars are any echinoderms belonging to the class Asteroidea. They typically have five 
or more ‘arms’ which radiate from a central disk in a symmetrical way. Most starfish have 5 arms, 
but some have more or fewer.
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a radiate 
b regenerate 
c spawning 
d buoyant
While starfish are commonly represented as having only 5 legs, there are some that exhibit 
many more, as you can see below. 
Nine Armed Starfish       Sunflower Starfish 
   Cushion Starfish     Spiny Beaded Starfish
2 
On each starfish shown above, draw a line to mark one axis of symmetry. Then draw at 
least two more lines to mark further axes of symmetry.
3 
How many legs on:
a 40 Nine Armed Starfish? 
b 34 Cushion Starfish? 
c 234 Spiny Beaded Starfish? 
d 321 Sunflower Starfish? 
e 45 Cushion Starfish? 
f 567 Sunflower Starfish?
4 
How many starfish are needed for each of these groups of legs?
a 243 Nine Armed Starfish legs 
b 1 197 Sunflower Starfish legs 
c 2 050 Cushion Starfish legs 
d 2 600 Spiny Beaded Starfish legs 
e 7 020 Nine Armed Starfish legs 
f 10 640 Sunflower Starfish legs 
5 
The underside of a starfish is covered with hundreds of tube feet. These are used for 
walking around, for attaching tightly to rocks and for holding on to prey. With so many 
little legs, some starfish can reach speeds of 120 centimetres per minute.
a How many centimetres per hour is this?
b How many metres per hour is this?
c How many kilometres per hour is this?
6 
The Crown of Thorns Starfish can move up to 600 m in a week. How fast on average is 
this, in metres per hour? 
Some species of starfish have the ability to regenerate lost arms and, over time, can grow 
an entire new arm. Most species must have the central part of the body intact in order to 
regenerate, but a few can grow an entire starfish from a single ray. 
ISBN  978 1 92571 009 0

© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009 
Maths in the Wild 
19
Exciting echinoderms - starfish (cont’d) 
8
7 
Calculate the percentage of starfish that grew new arms from the following batches 
examined by marine scientists.
a 203 out of 1900 
b 122 out of 1234 
c 163 out of 1825 
d 211 out of 2098 
e 102 out of 1291 
f 198 out of 2023
The Crown of Thorns Starfish has thorn-like spines sprouting all over its body for protection. 
These starfish grow to a diameter of more than 50 cm and have 12 to 20 arms extending from 
their centre. They are the largest starfish in the world, after the Giant Sunstar. The Crown of 
Thorns Starfish is a coral reef predator and preys on coral polyps. It is a serious threat to the 
coral on the Great Barrier Reef and on other coral reefs around the world. 
8 
It takes a Crown of Thorns Starfish 
about 5 hours to eat a small area of 
coral, about the size of a small plate. 
a If a small plate measures 6 cm in 
diameter, calculate the area of coral 
a Crown of Thorns Starfish can eat  
in one year.
b How much is this to the nearest 
square metre?
c Calculate the side length of a square this size.
d Use chalk to mark out the square on some flat concrete.
9 
The Crown of Thorns Starfish can release 20 million eggs in a summer spawning. Many 
of the eggs are lost due to poor fertilisation, predators and a lack of food. How many extra 
adult starfish are there, if for 20 million eggs there is a success rate of:
a 0.001% reaching adulthood? 
b 0.01% reaching adulthood? 
 
c 25% reaching adulthood?
The eggs of the Crown of Thorns Starfish (COT) are not buoyant and drop to the ocean floor. 
After 2 days, the starfish is 0.05 mm, after 6 months it is 20 mm, after 2 years it is 14 cm (and 
mature) and after 3 to 4 years it is about 35 cm in size and its growth declines dramatically. It 
is thought that these starfish can live for up to 8 years.
10 Draw a time versus size graph on the axis  
at the right to show the growth of the  
Crown of Thorns Starfish over its first  
5 years. (Use days on the horizontal axis.)
11 Use your graph to answer these questions.
a What is the diameter of a COT when  
it is 1 000 days old?
b What is the diameter of a COT when  
it is 500 days old?
c How old is a COT at 200 mm diameter?
d How old is a COT at 300 mm diameter?

uploads/mathematics/Maths in the Wild/09.subject: Mathematics
uploads/mathematics/Maths in the Wild/09.searchText:
20 
Maths in the Wild 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
Native fish - Golden Perch & Murray Cod 
9
The Golden Perch, commonly called a yellow belly, is a medium-to-large fish with a deep, laterally 
compressed body. It is considered rare in much of its original range, although it is still present in 
large numbers in many locations. Its maximum weight is 23 kg and maximum length is 760 mm, but 
it is usually less than 400 mm and 4 kg. The body colour is generally olive-green with a yellow or 
cream belly. The mouth is large, with the lower jaw protruding slightly. The tail is rounded.
Murray Cod are an Australian native fish. They were once widespread throughout the  
Murray-Darling system, and found in some surprisingly small streams. This species was the most 
common of the larger native fish in the Murray-Darling system at the time of European settlement. 
Wild stocks are now estimated to be less than ten percent of the population present at that time.
Whenever you see a colour code letter, find your answer in the shape at the end of the 
worksheet and colour that section. Colour code: R = red, B = blue, G = green, Y = yellow. 
1

d 8 kg 450 g =           g (G)

o 650 cm =        mm (G)

Golden Perch are predominantly found in warm, turbid, slow-flowing rivers. The species is 
long-lived, with a maximum age of about 25 years, although most live less than 11 years. 
Males are reproductively mature at 2 years and females at 4 years.
2 
Change these Golden Perch ages to the units shown.
a 25 yr =        wk (R) 
b 11 yr =        wk (G) 
c 2 yr 23 wk =        wk (Y)
d 4 yr 12 wk =        wk (G) 
e 3 wk =        d (R)

Adult and immature fish are migratory. Extensive upstream movements of more than  
1 000 kilometres have been recorded for some adult fish. Outside the breeding season, 
individuals occupy home ranges of about 100 m2 for weeks or months before relocating to 
another site where a new home range is established.
3 
Change these Golden Perch movements  
to the units shown.
a 500 km =        m 
b 600 km =        m 
c 450 km =        m 
d 1 000 km =        m
4 
Recent research in the Murray River suggests 
that some fish move downstream to spawn. 
Golden Perch are highly fecund, with a 2.3 kg  
female holding up to 500 000 eggs.  
Water-hardened eggs are large, about 3 mm 
diameter, semi-buoyant and drift downstream. 
Hatching occurs after 1 to 2 days and newly 
hatched larvae are about 3.5 mm long.

© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009

21
Native fish - Golden Perch & Murray Cod (cont’d) 
9
a If the Golden Perch eggs were laid side-by-side in a straight line, how far in metres 
would they reach?
b If all the eggs hatch and the larvae are laid end-to-end, how far in metres would they 
reach?
Murray Cod reach at least 60 cm and 3 to 4 kilograms in smaller streams. In larger rivers they 
grow to about 90 cm and weigh 20 kg. The largest Murray Cod ever officially recorded was 
183 cm and 113 kg. Unfortunately, excessive fishing has led to a serious lack of large, mature 
breeding cod in wild populations. There are now very few cod above the minimum legal 
angling size of 50 cm. Egg counts range from less than 10 000 eggs for a barely mature female 
to approximately 90 000 for older females, which weigh around 22 kg.
5 
How many eggs would be laid by these numbers of recently matured female cod?
a 8 cod 
b 9 cod 
c 12 cod 
d 20 cod 
e 27 cod
6 
How many eggs would be laid by these numbers of older female cod?
a 7 cod 
b 6 cod 
c 13 cod 
d 21 cod 
e 41 cod
The eggs of cod are large, about 3.5 mm in diameter, and sticky. They are usually deposited 
onto hard surfaces such as logs, rocks or clay banks. 
The male guards the eggs during incubation and they hatch after 5 to 13 days. The larvae are 
about 6 mm long at hatching and have a large yolk sac. Larvae drift downstream for 5 to 7 
days, particularly by night in spring and summer. 
7 
Change these cod life cycle times to the units shown. 
a 5 d =        hr 
b 13 d =        hr

For a long time, fish researchers believed that Murray Cod lived near a particular snag.  
Large Murray Cod were fitted with transmitting radio tags, revealing that they make  
strong upstream spawning migrations in late winter and spring. Many fish travelled  
40 to 50 kilometres upstream. Some travelled 120 kilometres upstream. 
Most Murray Cod returned downstream to the same snag after  
spawning migrations. This remarkable homing behaviour is  
almost unknown in freshwater fish and emphasises the  
importance of snags to Murray Cod.
8

22 
Maths in the Wild 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
A cute crustacean - yabbies 
10
The common yabby, Cherax Destructor, is an Australian freshwater crustacean. In the wild, yabby 
populations remain strong. They have moved into new habitats created by reservoirs and farm 
dams. Their colour depends on the water clarity and habitat they live in – yabbies can range from 
black, blue-black or dark brown in clear waters to light brown or green-brown in ‘dirty’ waters.
Yabbies occasionally reach up to 30 cm in 
length and up to 310 g in weight, but are more 
commonly 10 to 20 cm long. Like all crustaceans, 
yabbies have to moult as they grow. As they grow 
older, they moult less. After each moulting, their 
weight can increase by up to 50%.
1 
Calculate the new weight of each yabby if its 
weight increases by 40% after each moult.
a 20 g 
b 35 g  
c 25 g
d 58 g 
e 18 g
The number of fertilised eggs carried by the  
female yabby ranges from 100 to 300 for a young 
female to 1 100 for a larger, older female. The eggs 
are located under their tails.
2 
How many eggs could by carried by these numbers of older females?
a 5 yabbies 
b 10 yabbies 
c 15 yabbies 
d 12 yabbies 
e 20 yabbies
3 
How many eggs could be carried by these numbers of young females, if each one carries 
200 eggs?
a 5 yabbies 
b 10 yabbies 
c 15 yabbies 
d 12 yabbies 
e 20 yabbies
Juvenile yabbies are approximately 0.02 g upon hatching. The young yabby grows rapidly, 
gaining about 0.8 g in the first 60 days. The juvenile moults several times and continues to 
grow rapidly until it reaches adulthood and 80 grams after about 12 months. The maximum 
size of around 310 grams for adult yabbies is reached in 2 to 3 years. The minimum 
marketable size for yabbies is 30 grams, and this size can be reached in around 6 months.
4 
Draw a line graph to show the growth rate of the yabby. Mark in the marketable size.
5 
Use your graph to answer these questions.
a How heavy is a yabby aged 30 months?
b How old is a yabby that weighs 200 grams?
ISBN  978 1 92571 009 0

© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009 
Maths in the Wild 
23
A cute crustacean - yabbies (cont’d) 
10
Yabbies are commonly found on muddy or silted bottoms of dams and rivers. They are rarely 
found in clear water habitats, preferring muddy water. Muddy waters afford some protection 
from predators such as fish and birds, giving the yabby a better chance of survival. Optimal 
growth is achieved when water salinity (salt) levels are lower than 1 part salt to 125 parts 
water and the water is well oxygenated. 
6 
Calculate the ratio of salt to water (salinity level) of these samples of water.
a 16 parts of salt and 4 000 parts of water

Yabbies are capable of surviving in sea water for approximately 48 hours. However, high 
salinity levels result in increased stress and the yabby dies. In which samples of water in 
question 6 are the yabbies likely to survive?

The tail meat of a yabby is a popular food for many people. This portion makes up about 
15% of the total body weight when the yabby has been headed and shelled. Calculate the 
weight of tail meat that could be obtained from yabbies weighing:

yabbies per hectare of water. Calculate the expected yield from dams with these quantities 
of water:
a 3 ha

uploads/mathematics/Maths in the Wild/11.title: The Camelidae family - camels
uploads/mathematics/Maths in the Wild/11.subject: Mathematics
uploads/mathematics/Maths in the Wild/11.searchText:
24 
Maths in the Wild 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
There are two main types of camels – the Dromedary which 
is one-humped and the Bactrian Camel which has two humps. 
The term ‘camel’ is also used to describe any of the six  
camel-like creatures in the family camelidae. These are the 
two true camels and the four South American camelids:  
the Llama, Alpaca, Guanaco and Vicuña.
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a feral 
b dehydrated 
c hydrated 
d ingest
A fully-grown adult camel stands 1.85 m at the shoulder and 2.15 m at the hump. The hump 
rises about 60 cm from its body. 
2 
Change these camel measurements to the units shown.
a 2 m =         mm 
b 3 m =         mm 
c 1.85 m =         mm
d 2.15 m =         mm 
e 4 m =         cm 
f 3 m =         cm
g 1.85 m =         cm 
h 2.15 m =         cm
3 
Currently there is a large feral population of Dromedary Camels. This population is 
estimated at 700 000 in central Australia. These feral camels are descended from the 
camels that were introduced as a means of transport in the 19th century. The feral 
population is growing at approximately 11% per year. If growth rates remain constant, 
how many camels will exist in Australia:
a after 1 year? 
b after 2 years? 
c after 4 years?
4 
Camels are scattered throughout the arid interior of Australia, with an estimated 50% in 
Western Australia, 24% in the Northern Territory and 25% in western Queensland and 
northern South Australia. If there are 700 000 camels in total, how many are located in:
a Western Australia? 
b the Northern Territory? 
c all other parts of Australia?
Camels can withstand changes in body temperature and water content that would kill most 
other animals. Their body temperature can range from 34°C at night to 41°C during the day. 
Only above this threshold will they begin to sweat. The safe body temperature range for a 
human is 35.6°C to 37.2°C. 
5 
Write a temperature scale on the arrow below. Then shade the temperature ranges for a 
human and a camel. 
Camels can withstand a weight loss due to sweating of approximately 25%. Most mammals 
can only withstand 3.5% dehydration before heart failure results from the thickened blood.  
A camel’s blood remains hydrated, even though the body fluids are lost, until this 25% limit  
is reached.
The Camelidae family - camels 
11
ISBN  978 1 92571 009 0

© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009 
Maths in the Wild 
25
The Camelidae family - camels (cont’d) 
11
6 
Calculate the maximum safe weight loss for a camel of each weight listed. 
a 300 kg 
b 550 kg 
c 220 kg 
d 350 kg 
e 490 kg
7 
Calculate the maximum safe weight loss in these other mammals if they weigh:
a 85 kg 
b 90 kg 
c 210 kg 
d 350 kg 
e 490 kg
Camels eating green herbage can ingest sufficient moisture in milder conditions to maintain 
their body’s hydrated state without needing to drink. In extremely dry areas, they need access 
to water holes. A thirsty camel can drink 200 litres in three minutes. It can drink water that is 
too salty or brackish for other animals to drink.
8 
How much water can a camel drink in:
a 6 min? 
b 9 min? 
c 1 min? 
d 5 min? 
e 2 min 30 s?
9 
How long would it take a camel to drink:
a 400 L? 
b 800 L? 
c 100 L? 
d 120 L? 
e 250 L?
A camel carcass can provide a substantial amount of meat. The male Dromedary carcass 
can weigh 400 kg or more, while the carcass of a male Bactrian can weigh up to 650 kg. The 
carcass of a female camel weighs less than the male, at about 330 kg. The hump is considered 
to be a delicacy.  
10 How much meat could be obtained from these numbers of male camels, in tonnes?
a 5 Dromedary Camels 
b 7 Bactrian Camels 
c 12 Bactrian Camels 
d 9 Dromedary Camels 
11 How many female camels are needed to supply these quantities of meat?
a 660 kg 
b 990 kg 
c 1200 kg 
d 3 tonne
Feral camels wander widely according to the conditions. Sometimes they cover 70 kilometres 
in a single day. They would only travel half this distance if they were working in a camel 
train, carrying large loads.
12 How long would it take a feral camel to travel:
a 140 km? 
b 350 km? 
c 700 km? 
d 820 km? 
e 1500 km?
13 How far could a working camel walk in: 
a 4 days? 
b 5 days? 
c 12 days? 
d 3 weeks? 
e 5 weeks?
14 Large camel trains consist of about 65 camels and 5 camel handlers. A large bull camel is 
expected to carry up to 600 kg and small camels to carry about 350 kg. How much weight 
could these camels carry, in tonnes?
a 4 bulls 
b 7 bulls 
c 6 small camels 
d 4 bulls and 3 small camels  
e 3 bulls and 5 small camels
15 All camels moult in spring and grow a new coat by autumn. Camel hair is used for high-
quality coats, garments and artist’s brushes. A camel can shed 2.25 kilograms of hair at 
each moult.
a How much hair is lost by 60 camels at a single moult? 
b How many camels are needed to produce 40 kg of camel hair after one moulting?

Maths in the Wild 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
Silent and deadly – snakes and scorpions 
12
A snake is a long reptile, covered in scales. All snakes are carnivores. Snakes do not have eyelids, 
limbs, external ears or legs. While venomous snakes comprise a minority of the species, some 
possess potent venom that is capable of causing painful injury or death to humans. However, venom 
in snakes is primarily used for killing or subduing prey, rather than for self defence.
Scorpions are eight-legged carnivorous arthropods and there are about 2000 species of scorpions. 
Most scorpions are relatively harmless to humans, with their stings only resulting in pain, 
numbness or swelling. However, a few scorpion species, mostly in the family Buthidae, can be 
dangerous to humans.
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a venom 
b toxic  
c neurotoxin
Snake venoms are like soups. Most of them contain many 
different components and some of these are toxic to people. 
For example, in the venom of the Common Tiger Snake, 
there are at least 6 neurotoxins which affect the human 
nervous system.  
2 
The table lists the relative toxicity of snake venoms. 
Plot a picture graph, using snakes as columns, to 
compare the toxicity of the venoms.
3 
How many times more toxic is the venom of: 
a a Common Brown Snake than the Common Tiger 
Snake?
b an Inland Taipan than the Red-bellied Black Snake?
c a Taipan than the King Cobra?
d a Common Tiger Snake than the Western Brown snake?
4 
The moulting of a snake’s skin serves two main functions – to replace the old and 
worn skin and to help get rid of parasites such as mites and ticks. Moulting is repeated 
periodically throughout a snake’s life. An older snake might shed its skin twice a year. A 
younger, still-growing snake might shed four times a year. If a snake reaches maturity in 
2 years and lives for 10 years, how many times is it likely to shed its skin?
5 
Pythons are a family of non-venomous snakes. Among its members are some of the 
largest snakes in the world. Adults range in size from 0.5 m to 10 m in length. The 
Reticulated Python holds the record of 10 m for the world’s longest snake. Change these 
Python lengths to the units shown.

Despite their awesome size, Pythons are not poisonous. They are excellent swimmers and 
can cover great distances in small amounts of time. Scientists trapped some Pythons and 
equipped them with radio transmitters. These Pythons swam 60 kilometres in three hours. 
Calculate the average swimming speed of Pythons that swim:
a 30 km in 3 hr

10 Scorpions prefer to live in areas where the temperature ranges from 20°C to 37°C. They 
can survive the freezing temperatures and scorching heat of the deserts. Write a scale on

Scorpions take a long time to reach maturity. As they grow, they moult 6 times per year. A 
scorpion generally lives two to ten years. Some have been recorded as living for up to 25 years.
13 If a scorpion lived for ten years and moulted twice each adult year, how many times 
would it moult given that it reached maturity in: 
a 4 years?

The tiger is a mammal of the Felidae family and is native to much of eastern and southern Asia. It 
can grow up to 4 metres long and weigh up to 300 kilograms. Aside from great bulk and power, the 
tiger’s most recognisable feature is the pattern of dark vertical stripes overlaying near-white to 
reddish-orange fur. 
Whenever you see a colour code letter, find your answer in the shape at the end of the 
worksheet and colour that section. Colour code: R = red, B = blue, G = green, Y = yellow. 
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a deciduous 
b mangrove  
c mutation
2 
In the 1920s, about 100 000 tigers existed in the wild. In the 1990s, five different scientists 
made these estimates of the wild tiger population: 4840, 7040, 6270, 5010 and 6540. 
Calculate the average estimate of wild tiger numbers.
3 
Of the tigers surveyed, it was estimated that 3100 of these were Bengal Tigers, 400 were 
Siberian, 500 were Sumatrans, 1200 were Indo-Chinese, 40 were South Chinas and  
700 were Malay Tigers. Calculate the average percentage of these tiger species making up 
the existing numbers.
a Bengal 
b Siberians 
c Sumatrans 
d Indo-Chinese 
e South Chinas 
f Malay
4 
a Calculate the average percentage reduction in tiger numbers from 1920 to 1990.
b Suggest why there has been such a decrease in tiger populations.
5 
The Bengal Tiger is found in parts of India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan and Burma. It 
lives in varied habitats: grasslands, subtropical and tropical rainforests, scrub forests, wet 
and dry deciduous forests and mangroves. Males in the wild usually weigh about 210 kg  
while the average female weighs about 140 kg. Conservationists have estimated the 
current number of Bengal Tigers to be 1400 – 40% of their population 10 years ago. 
a How many Bengal Tigers were there 10 years ago?
b How much heavier is the male than the female, as a percentage? (R)
6 
The Indo-Chinese Tiger is found in Cambodia, China, Laos, Burma, Thailand and 
Vietnam. These tigers are smaller and darker than Bengal Tigers. Males weigh about  
170 kg while females are smaller at 125 kg. Estimates of the total Indo-Chinese Tiger 
population are 1 500, with about three hundred left in the wild.
a What percentage of Indo-Chinese Tigers lives in the wild? (B)
b What percentage of Indo-Chinese Tigers lives in captivity? (Y)
c How much lighter is the female than the male, as a percentage? (Y)
7 
Sumatran Tigers are found only on the Indonesian island of Sumatra. They are close 
to extinction. Sumatran Tigers are the smallest of all living tiger subspecies, with adult 
males weighing about 110 kg and females about 80 kg. The wild population is estimated 
to be 450. Habitat destruction is the main threat to the existing tiger population – 
however, about 60 tigers were recorded as being shot and killed between 1998 and 2000.
a What percentage of the wild population of tigers was shot and killed between 1998 and 
2000? (G)
b How much heavier is the male tiger than the female tiger, as a percentage? (R)

the wild but widely bred in zoos due to its popularity. White tigers can only be born when 
both parents carry a rare gene. This gene has been calculated to occur in only one in 
every 10 000 births. What percentage of births is this? (R)

Adult tigers are fiercely territorial. The size of a tiger’s home range mainly depends on 
prey abundance but also, in the case of male tigers, on access to females. A tigress may

1 second? (Y)
