uploads/mathematics/Maths in the Wild/14.subject: Mathematics
uploads/mathematics/Maths in the Wild/14.searchText:
30 
Maths in the Wild 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
The lion is a member of the family Felidae, and one of four big cats in the genus Panthera. With 
exceptionally large males exceeding 250 kg in weight, it is the second-largest living cat after the 
tiger. Wild lions currently exist in Africa and Asia, with a critically endangered population in north-
west India. They have disappeared from North Africa, the Middle East and Western Asia.
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a defecating 
b synchronise 
c scavenging
Weights for adult lions generally lie between 150 and 250 kg for males, and 120 and 180 kg 
for females. Head and body length is 170 to 250 cm for males and 140 to 170 cm for females. 
Shoulder height is about 125 cm in males and 100 cm in females. 
2 
For these adult lions, calculate the midpoint of the given ranges for the:
a weight of a male. 
b weight of a female. 
c length of a male. 
d length of a female.
3 
Use the midpoints you calculated in the previous question to draw rectangles to represent 
a male and female lion. Use a scale of 1:100.
Lions spend much of their time resting, and are inactive for about 20 hours per day. Although 
lions can be active at any time, their activity generally peaks after dusk with a period of 
socialising, grooming and defecating. Hunting most often takes place at dawn. Each day, lions 
spend an average of two hours walking and 50 minutes eating.
4 
On average: 
a how many minutes per day are spent resting?
b how many minutes per day are spent walking?
c how many hours per day are spent eating?
d how many seconds per day are spent eating?
5 
On average, what percentage of a lion’s day is spent:
a resting? 
b walking? 
c eating?
Lions can reach speeds of 60 km/h for short bursts. They sneak up to within 30 m of their prey 
before launching an attack. Lions generally prey on medium size animals such as zebras, 
gazelle and wildebeest. On average, they are only successful in five out of twenty attempts. A 
lioness uses her weight and paws to knock her quarry down. She then secures the meal with a 
bite to the throat or neck, generally suffocating the victim. If a lioness cannot catch her prey 
in the first few hundred metres, she gives up and chooses another victim.
6 
Change these lion speeds to m/s.
a 120 km/h 
b 90 km/h 
c 40 km/h 
d 60 km/h 
e 100 km/h
7 
At 60 km/h, how long would it take a lion to run these distances to catch its prey?
a 20 m 
b 30 m 
c 35 m 
d 40 m 
e 60 m 
8 
How many times is a lion likely to be successful at catching prey in these numbers of 
attempts?
a 20 
b 60 
c 120 
d 16 
e 24
Queens and kings of the jungle - lions 
14
ISBN  978 1 92571 009 0

© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009 
Maths in the Wild 
31
A lion can gorge itself, eating up to 30 kg in one sitting. If it is unable to eat the entire kill, 
it will rest for a few hours before eating more. On a hot day, the pride may retreat to shade, 
leaving a male or two to stand guard. An adult lioness requires an average of 5 kg of meat per 
day, a male 7 kg.
9 
On average, how much meat will these lions need to eat over the time shown?
a A male, 12 days 
b A male, 3 weeks 
c A female, 23 days 
d A female, 2 months
10 On average, how many equivalent ‘days of meat’ are these amounts for a lioness? 
a 30 kg 
b 25 kg 
c 10 kg 
d 12 000 g
11 Scavenging makes up about 12% of a lion’s food source. Lions listen for vultures and 
hyenas, which are scavengers, and go to the scene to take what they can for themselves. 
How much food is likely to be scavenged by these lions during the given time?
a 1 male, 12 wks 
b 2 males, 10 wks 
c 1 female, 16 wks 
d 3 females, 1 yr
12 Most lions now live in eastern and southern Africa. Their numbers have rapidly decreased 
over the last two decades. One current estimate of the African lion population is 31 000, 
living in the wild. This has decreased from 100 000 in 1990 and 400 000 in 1950.
a Draw a line graph to show the changes in the wild African lion population since 1950. 
b Calculate the percentage decrease in the lion population since 1950. 
c Suggest why the number of lions has been decreasing.
d From your graph, what was the lion population in 1970?   
 
e From your graph, when was the lion population 150 000?
Like lion numbers, habitat for lions has declined over the past two decades. Since the 1960s, 
the human population, land cultivation and number of livestock have steadily increased. In 
2001, scientists estimated the habitat for lions was about 5 200 000 km2, and suggested that 
this is half of that available in the 1950s. More detailed estimates suggest that the lion habitat 
is approximately three million km2, with about half of this area protected by a national park 
or reserve. Much of the lion’s habitat is fragmented and unprotected.
13 a What area of land was available for lion habitat in the 1950s?
b Find the length ‘x ’ of the rectangle below  
given that its area is 10 400 000 km2.
c Draw this rectangle to scale on  
the map of Australia.
d Shade a square of area  
3 000 000 km2 on the map.
e From detailed estimates, what  
percentage of the lion’s habitat  
is protected by national parks and reserves?
14 Explain the significance of the lion’s habitat  
being fragmented and unprotected.
500 km

32 
Maths in the Wild 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
The smallest bee is the dwarf bee, Trigona Minima, which is about 2.1 mm long. The largest bee in 
the world is Megachile Pluto, which can grow to about 40 mm in length. 
In Australia, the first European Wasps were found in Tasmania in 1959. By 1978 they had also been 
found in Victoria, South Australia, New South Wales and Western Australia. European Wasps are 
more aggressive than bees and will attack when their nests are disturbed.  
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a forage 
b pollen 
c pollination 
d nectar  
e wax
2 
Draw pictures of the Trigona Minima bee and the  
Megachile Pluto bee, using a scale of 2:1.
Honeybees live in hives or colonies. A small hive contains about 
20 000 bees, while larger hives can have 120 000 bees. Hives 
include one queen, hundreds of drones and thousands of worker 
bees. The worker bees are female and do not breed. The queen 
bee is female and creates all the babies for the hive. The drone 
bees are male and do not have stingers. 
3 
How many honeybees live in these small hives?
a 3 
b 5 
c 12 
d 23 
e 65
4 
How many large hives are needed to support these numbers of bees?
a 240 000 
b 600 000 
c 200 000 
d 900 000 
e 2 million
The worker bees collect pollen and nectar from flowers. The pollen is used as a protein source 
and the nectar is an energy source. Bees turn the nectar into honey. Workers visit about four 
thousand flowers to make one tablespoon of honey. Beekeepers are very careful when they 
remove honey from the hive. They try not to hurt the bees and leave sugar syrup to replace 
the honey they take.
5 
Calculate the quantity of honey, in tablespoons, produced from bees visiting these 
numbers of flowers.
a 8 000 
b 12 000 
c 40 000 
d 15 000 
e 26 000
6 
If a tablespoon of honey weighs 30 g, how many tablespoons make up one kilogram?
7 
Calculate the number of flowers visited to make these quantities of honey.
a 30 g 
b one kilogram 
c 3 kg 
d 20 kg 
e 170 g
There are about 80 000 commercial bee hives in Queensland. Each hive produces about 70 
kilograms of honey. The Queensland bee industry supplies honey, beeswax, honeycomb, 
queen bee exports and pollination services. 
8 
Assume that 133 320 flowers produce 1 kg of honey. For a hive to produce 70 kg of honey, 
how many flowers does a single bee have to visit if, in its hive, there are:
a 20 thousand workers? 
b 50 thousand workers?
9 
Calculate the annual production of honey in Queensland, in:
a kilograms. 
b tonnes.
Stings and wings - bees and wasps 
15
ISBN  978 1 92571 009 0

© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009

33
Stings and wings - bees and wasps (cont’d) 
15
10 If honey is valued at $4 per kilogram, calculate the total value of honey produced. 
11 One hundred tonnes of beeswax are produced each year. Calculate the value of 
production at $4.50 per kilogram.
12 Queen bees are valued at $16 each. If 25 000 are exported, what is the total value of sales?
13 Calculate the total value of sales of honey, beeswax and queen bee exports from the bee 
industry.
In Australia, the temperatures are warm enough for worker 
European Wasps to survive the winter. This means that if a 
new queen remains in her old nest, the nest does not begin 
with a single individual, but with a new queen and several 
thousand workers. These nests are called ‘overwintering’ 
nests and by summer can increase in size to house over  
100 000 worker wasps.
14 By summer, how many wasps could be in these  
numbers of nests?
a 4 
b 6 
c 8 
d 12 
e 23
15 How many nests are needed to house these numbers of worker wasps?
a 500 000 
b 600 000 
c 700 000 
d 850 000 
e 950 000
16 Wasp larvae are fed and checked by ‘nursing’ adult workers about 65 times each hour. 
Total larval development time is about 22 days, depending on the temperature and 
availability of food.
a Approximately, how many times per minute does an adult worker check the larvae?
b How many times would the larvae be checked over 22 days of development time?
17 European Wasps usually forage for food within 50 to 250 metres of their nest, although in 
some instances they have been recorded flying several kilometres for food. If you have a 
large number of European Wasps interrupting your outdoor activities, then you probably 
have a nest nearby. Calculate the total forage area for these spaces. 
a  
b  
c

stings is relatively low in Australia.

uploads/mathematics/Maths in the Wild/16.subject: Mathematics
uploads/mathematics/Maths in the Wild/16.searchText:
34 
Maths in the Wild 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
Mosquitoes are insects that make up the family Culicidae. They have a pair of scaled wings, a pair of 
halteres, a slender body and long legs. The females of most mosquito species suck blood from other 
animals. This has made them the most deadly disease carriers we know. They have killed millions of 
people over thousands of years and continue to kill millions per year by spreading diseases.
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a halteres  
b pupae
2 
Mosquitoes can grow to 16 mm in length and 2.5 mg in weight. 
a How long can mosquitoes grow, in centimetres?
b How many mozzies are needed to make up 1 gram of mozzie flesh?
3 
A mosquito can fly continuously for 1 to 4 hours at speeds of 2 km/h. They are capable of 
travelling more than 110 km from their breeding sites.
a How far could a mosquito travel in 4 hours?
b How far could a mosquito travel in one night, without resting? (Allow 6 hours of 
darkness.)
c How long would it take a mosquito to travel 110 km, without resting?
d How long would it take a mosquito to travel 110 km if it had a 5 km/h assisting breeze 
and no rests?
4 
Most species of mosquito feed at night or at dusk or dawn. During the heat of the day, 
most mosquitoes rest in a cool place but might still bite if disturbed. After drinking blood, 
adult females lay a raft of up to 400 (depending on the species) tiny, white eggs in still or 
very slow-moving water. How many eggs could these numbers of mosquitoes lay?
a 5 
b 6 
c 18 
d 23
Most eggs hatch into larvae in about 48 hours. As they grow, they shed or moult their skin 
about four times, growing larger after each moulting. The larvae eat micro-organisms and 
organic matter in the water. Mosquito larvae, commonly called ‘wrigglers’, must live in water 
for about 10 days, depending on the water’s temperature. The pupae are lighter than water, 
and float on the surface while changing into adult mosquitoes over about two days. The 
newly emerged adult rests on the surface of the water for a short time to allow itself to dry and 
all its parts to harden before it can fly. A mosquito’s adult life is about ten weeks.  
5 
Use the information above to  
label the diagram of the mosquito 
life cycle. 
6 
What is the total time, in hours, 
for a mosquito to complete its  
life cycle?
Over the past 20 million years or so, 
mosquitoes have been honing their 
hunting skills. They are now experts at 
finding people to bite. Mosquitoes have 
a battery of sensors designed to track 
prey. They can sense carbon dioxide 
and lactic acid from up to 40 metres 
away. 
Blood suckers - mosquitoes 
16
ISBN  978 1 92571 009 0

© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009 
Maths in the Wild 
35
Certain chemicals in sweat also seem to attract mosquitoes.  
If you are wearing clothing that contrasts with the 
background, especially if you move while wearing that 
clothing, mosquitoes can see you and zero in on you. 
Mosquitoes detect heat, so they can find warm-blooded 
mammals and birds easily once they get close enough.
7 
Mosquitoes were observed at these distances from 
a mammal. For each distance, decide whether the 
mosquito is likely to smell the mammal. 
a 30 m 
b 45 m 
c 5 000 cm
d 30 000 mm 
e 0.05 km 
f 0.02 km
Repellents like DEET work by disorienting the mosquito as it gets close to its potential next 
meal, but do not kill mosquitoes. Surprisingly, this works about 95% of the time. 
8 
How many successes is a mosquito likely to have if it makes these numbers of attacks on a 
person wearing DEET?
a 50                 b  36 
c 120              d  59 
e 12               f  250
9 
The concentrated mosquito repellent DEET is mixed in with water. Low concentrations of 
DEET are sufficient for most outdoor protection. A 15% concentration is recommended for 
most purposes. Which of these repellent mixtures would be satisfactory for most purposes?
a 50 mL water, 10 mL DEET 
b 110 mL water, 20 mL DEET
c 120 mL water, 17 mL DEET
In Australia, diseases transmitted by mosquitoes include Dengue fever, Australian 
encephalitis, Ross River fever and Barmah Forest virus disease. Ross River fever and Barmah 
Forest virus disease have a wide variety of symptoms, from rashes with fevers to arthritis that 
can last from months to years. Ross River fever is the most commonly reported mosquito-
transmitted disease in all states of Australia. Malaria is rare in Australia.
10 The table at the right shows the number of reported 
infections of Ross River fever in South Australia.
a Complete the third column of the table, then draw a 
sector graph to compare the number of infections  
each year. 
b Which year had the most infections?
c Which year had the least infections?
d Suggest an explanation for the nature of the graph  
you drew.
11 The table below shows the numbers of males and females 
infected with Ross River fever in South Australia. 
a What is the simplest ratio 
of infected males to infected 
females?

infected than females?

uploads/mathematics/Maths in the Wild/17.subject: Mathematics
uploads/mathematics/Maths in the Wild/17.searchText:
36 
Maths in the Wild 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
A bird of prey, or raptor, is a bird that hunts for food primarily on the wing, using its amazing sense 
of vision. The talons and beaks of raptors tend to be relatively large and powerful, and adapted for 
tearing or piercing the flesh of their victims.
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a altitude 
b juveniles
The Wedge-tailed Eagle is Australia’s largest living bird of prey and one of the largest eagles 
in the world. It reaches about 1.0 m in length and has a wingspan of 2.3 m. Females are 
larger than males – they average 4.2 kg in weight with males at about 3.2 kg. This eagle has 
a characteristic long, wedge-shaped tail, and legs that are feathered all the way to the base of 
the toes.
2

a 2 m =            cm 
b 1.0 m =            cm 
c 2.3 m =            cm 
d 430 cm =            m 
e 450 cm =            m
Australia’s second largest eagle, the White-bellied Sea Eagle, has shorter, more rounded wings 
than the Wedge-tailed Eagle and no feathers on its lower legs. The White-bellied Sea Eagle is 
about 0.8 m long with a wingspan of roughly 2.2 m. Males weigh close to 3.1 kg and females 
3.5 kg.
3 
Change these eagle weights to the units shown.
a 3 kg =            g 
b 2 kg =            g 
c 2.3 kg =            g  
d 4000 g =            kg 
e 5200 g =            kg
Eagles can be seen perched on trees or poles or soaring overhead at altitudes up to 2000 m.  
An eagle’s nest is a large structure of dead sticks, usually reused for years and often reaching 
considerable sizes. Over many years, a nest can be built up to 1.8 m across, 3 m deep and 
about 400 kg in weight. 
4 
Change these measurements to the units shown.
a 2000 m =            km 
b 2300 m =            km 
c 600 m =            km 
d 3 km =            m 
e 1.6 km =            m 
f 3000 kg =            t 
g 3200 kg =            t 
h 400 kg =            t 
i 5 t =            kg 
The diet of the Wedge-tailed Eagle reflects the available prey, but the most important live 
items are rabbits and hares. Rabbits usually comprise 55% of the diet, but might comprise up 
to 90%. Other food items include lizards, birds, foxes, feral cats and other mammals. Lambs 
comprise less than 10% of an eagle’s total diet, with most of the sheep meat consumed sourced 
from carcasses, dying sheep or road fatalities. Less than 2% of all lambs killed are the result of 
an eagle’s attack; foxes and crows account for the remainder. 
5 
The average daily requirement of food for a captive adult eagle is about 600 g.
a If rabbit makes up 55% of the eagle’s diet, what is the weight of rabbit needed per day?
b If rabbit makes up 90% of the eagle’s diet, what is the weight of rabbit needed per day?
c If 200 lambs are lost to predators, how many are likely to be lost to eagles?
d If 500 lambs are lost to predators, how many are likely to be lost to foxes and crows?

weight these eagles can lift. 
a a female Wedge-tailed Eagle 
b a male Wedge-tailed Eagle
c a female Sea Eagle 
d a male Sea Eagle
7 
The diet of the Sea Eagle consists mainly of live fish and sea snakes. These two sources 
account for about 90% of their diet. A Sea Eagle needs approximately 400 g of food per 
day. Calculate the weight of fish and sea snakes in a Sea Eagle’s daily diet.
Each pair of eagles occupies a home range, which may be as little as 9 square kilometres or as 
large as 120 square kilometres. This large home range is often shared with other eagle pairs 
for the purpose of hunting.

a

would have to fly from the nest to reach the edge of these home range areas:

especially starlings, galahs and rosellas. The Peregrine Falcon has a body length of 43 cm 
and a wingspan of around 100 cm. The female is up to 30 percent larger than the male. 
Males weigh about 450 g to 750 g, and females weigh 900 g to 1500 g. It is thought that 
the Peregrine Falcon can dive at speeds of around 360 kilometres per hour. 
a Calculate the dive speed of the Peregrine Falcon in m/s.
b If a falcon is 200 m above its prey, how long would it take the falcon to dive to its prey?
c If a falcon is 550 m above its prey, how long would it take the falcon to dive to its prey?

falcons die in their first year.

38 
Maths in the Wild 
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
On Christmas Day in 1859, the Victorian Acclimatisation Society released 24 rabbits to hunt for 
sport, to help settlers feel more ‘at home’.  By 1886, rabbits had spread as far as the Queensland-
NSW border and by 1900 they reached Western Australia and the Northern Territory. In the next 
60 years, rabbits invaded 4 million square kilometres of Australia, making it one of the fastest 
colonising mammals anywhere in the world. Rabbits are small mammals in the family Leporidae.
The European Red Fox was introduced to Victoria by fox hunters in 1871 and declared a pest in that 
state by 1901. Foxes crossed the border into NSW around 1893 and were declared a pest there soon 
after. They had spread through most of Australia by 1930.
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a colonising 
b myxomatosis  
c warren
2 
The smallest rabbit is the Pygmy Rabbit at only 20 cm in length and 0.4 kg in weight. The 
largest rabbits grow to 50 cm and more than 10 kg. Calculate the total weight of: 
a 6 Pygmy Rabbits and 6 of the largest rabbits. 
b 5 Pygmy Rabbits and 7 of the largest rabbits.
3 
Many people use the expression ‘breed like rabbits’. Rabbits have an extremely high 
reproductive potential. They are able to have their first litter at 3 months of age and then 
give birth to litters of 6 young every six weeks. Calculate the number of rabbits that can 
be reproduced during one year by:
a a single adult pair.  
b a single adult pair and their offspring.
4 
Two thousand rabbit warrens were ‘ripped’ in Jacko’s paddock, which can maintain  
700 sheep. The number of rabbits per warren varies from 10 to 50, depending on the 
amount of green feed available. Ten rabbits eat as much as one sheep. 
Calculate:
a the average number of rabbits on Jacko’s paddock, if there are 30 rabbits per warren.
b the number of sheep that could have eaten the amount of food the rabbits ate. 
5 
In grass plains, two hectares are required to support one sheep. For each paddock, 
calculate the area (in hectares) and the number of sheep it can support. (1 ha = 10 000 m2).
a  
b  
c
6 
At a recent sheep sale, sheep were sold for $95 each. If there are 2 rabbits per hectare in 
the paddocks in question 5, calculate the value of lost production to each farmer.
Commercial harvesting, including hunting, has not been effective in reducing wild rabbit 
numbers to protect natural resources. Shooting may remove a portion of the population but 
these are quickly replaced by reproduction. Rabbit shooters harvest only 1.5% of the rabbit 
population. Even after a 70% reduction in population size, rabbits can regain their former 
numbers within a single year.

small stomachs for their size and can only eat about 10% of their body weight in food

© Denis Day and Blake Education 2009
The Cane Toad (Bufo marinus) is also known as the Giant Neotropical Toad or Marine Toad. It is 
a large, terrestrial true toad native to Central and South America. Cane Toads were introduced 
to Australia to eat cane beetles. The ‘whitegrub’ larvae of these beetles eat the roots of sugar 
cane and kill or stunt the plants. About 100 toads were imported from Hawaii to the Meringa 
Experimental Station near Cairns. The toads bred quickly and more than 3 000 were released in  
the sugar cane plantations of north Queensland in July 1935. 
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a parotid  
b arthritis
By 2002, Cane Toads had spread throughout the eastern and northern half of Queensland. 
They have now extended their range to the river catchments surrounding Kakadu National 
Park, near Katherine, in the Northern Territory. In New South Wales they occur on the coast as 
far south as Yamba and there is an isolated colony near Port Macquarie. 
2 
From the map, how far is it from:
a Perth to Newman? 
b Brisbane to Cairns?
c Melbourne to Sydney? 
d Melbourne to Brisbane?
e Adelaide to Darwin?
3

is the direction from:
a Darwin to Katherine? 
b Adelaide to Melbourne?

the Cane Toad now inhabits. 
5

a in a westerly direction. 
b in a southerly direction.
During the day and in cold or dry weather, Cane Toads shelter in moist crevices and hollows, 
sometimes excavating holes beneath logs, rocks and debris. They can survive the loss of up to 
50% of their body water, and survive temperatures ranging from 5 to 40ºC. 
6

dehydration?

Average-sized adult toads are about 15 cm long. The largest female measured in Queensland 
was 24 cm long and weighed 1.3 kg. Male Cane Toads are smaller and wartier than females.  
In other countries, Cane Toads have been recorded at 35 cm long and 2.6 kg in weight.
8

Juvenile toads lack the adults’ large parotid glands, so they are usually less poisonous. 
Because they lack this key defence, only about 0.5% of those that hatch from eggs survive to 
reach sexual maturity and reproduce. 
9

a 8 000 
b 20 000

b 320 
c 450

11 Cane Toads occupy more than 500 000 square kilometres of Australia and have reached 
densities of 2 000 toads per hectare in newly-colonised areas of the Northern Territory. 
However, the average density of toads in areas where they have been established for more 
than 20 years is much lower – about 80 toads per hectare in coastal Queensland towns. 
How many toads would be in the areas below which are near coastal Queensland towns?
a  
b

12 The toads on the western frontier of the Cane Toad advance have evolved larger legs.  
This is thought to be related to their ability to travel further. As a consequence of their 
longer legs, larger bodies and faster movement, about 10% of the leading edge of Cane 
Toads have also developed arthritis. It is estimated that Cane Toads migrate at an average 
of 40 kilometres per year.

Maths in the Wild

A pelican is any one of several large water birds with a distinctive pouch under the beak. Pelicans 
belong to the bird family Pelecanidae. Darters, cormorants, gannets, bobbies, frigatebirds and 
tropicbirds also belong to the pelican family. Pelicans are found on all continents except Antarctica.
Swans are large water birds of the family Anatidae, which also includes geese and ducks. Swans are 
closely related to geese, and scientists group the two in the tribe Cygnini.
1 
Find the meaning of each word listed below.  
a monogamous 
b gliding 
c soaring
Pelicans are large birds with enormous, pouched bills. The smallest is the Brown Pelican, 
which can weigh as little as 2.5 kg and have a wingspan of as little as 1.8 m. The largest is 
believed to be the Dalmatian Pelican, at up to 15 kg with a maximum wingspan of nearly  
3.5 m. The Australian Pelican weighs about 5.5 kg and has a wing span of approximately  
2.4 m – its 45 cm bill is the longest of any bird. 
2 
a Using the scale, label each pelican’s wing span with its length. 
b Identify and label each pelican. 
c The average human has an arm span of 173 cm. Draw a human with outstretched 
arms beside the pelicans above, using the same scale. 
3

Pelicans are colonial breeders, with up to 50 000 individuals grouping on islands or secluded 
shores. Breeding may occur at any time of year, depending on environmental conditions, 
particularly rainfall. All pelican species lay at least two eggs. Hatching success for undisturbed 
pairs can be as high as 95 percent, but because of competition between siblings, usually all 
nestlings but one die  
within the first few weeks.

After about a month, chicks leave their nests to form crèches. After two months, they have 
learnt to fly and are fairly independent. Wild birds live between 10 and 25 years, or more.

a 2 years?

weight. Calculate the skeleton weight of these pelicans, in grams.
a 2.5 kg 
b 3.6 kg 
c 15 kg 
d 5.5 kg
8 
When fully extended, the bill of a pelican can hold up to 13 litres of water. How many  
2 litre milk bottles would this fill?
Pelicans are highly mobile, searching out suitable areas of water and an adequate supply  
of food. A layer of special fibres deep in the breast muscles holds the wings rigidly horizontal 
for gliding and soaring. Pelicans are not capable of sustained flapping flight, but can remain 
in the air for 24 hours at a time. Flight at a height of 1 000 m is common, and heights of  
3 000 m have been recorded. By moving from one thermal air current to the next, pelicans 
can travel long distances with a minimum of effort and reach air speeds of 50 km/h. 
9 
How far could a pelican travel in 24 hours?
10 Change these heights to the units shown.

a the average weight of these 6 swans: 6 kg, 9 kg, 8.6 kg, 8.3 kg, 7 600 g, 5 500 g. 
b the average wing span of these 7 swans: 1.6 m, 2 m, 170 cm, 190 cm, 1.5 m, 175 cm, 
215 cm.
A Black Swan nest is essentially a large heap or mound of reeds, grasses and weeds. It is about 
1.2 m in diameter and up to 1 metre high, and positioned in shallow water or on an island. 
The nest is re-used every year, restored or rebuilt as needed.

13 Like other swans, the Black Swan is largely  
monogamous and pairs for life. However, they  
do have an average divorce rate of 5%.  
Calculate the average number of pairs of swans  
divorcing in:
a 340 pairs. 
b 280 pairs.

Since 1915, one day in the year has involved the whole of Australia in solemn ceremonies of 
remembrance, gratitude and national pride. That day is Anzac Day – 25 April.
Ten weeks after the beginning of World War 1, Australia and New Zealand sent 30 000 troops 
to Egypt for combat training. It was here that the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps 
acronym ANZAC was first used. At 3 am, on April 25 1914 just off the shores of Gallipoli in 
Turkey, in an area later to be known as Anzac Cove, three battleships gathered full of Anzac 
soldiers about to head into history. HMAS Queen, HMAS London and HMAS Prince of Wales 
released 48 boats or ‘tows’ at 3.30 am and the landings continued from 5.30 to 7.30 am. But 
something went wrong. The landings were over 2 km north of the intended area – a 6 km 
stretch of beach from about 1.6 km north of Gaba Tepe to a point near Fisherman’s Hut.

Hard tack and the Anzacs 
2
Besides the constant fear of death on the hills and dunes of Gallipoli, some logistical challenges 
included feeding the soldiers. Food supplies came from as far away as Greece and Egypt and 
perishables just wouldn’t survive. The soldiers’ food came in tins with the staples being corned beef 
(Bully Beef), rice, tea, cocoa, jam and ‘hard tack’. Hard tack is basically a very hard biscuit made 
of flour, water, salt and sugar. It lasts longer than bread, although it was so hard soldiers would 
sometimes break their teeth trying to eat it.
Unlike bread, hard tack biscuits are very, very hard. Some soldiers preferred to grind them up 
with old ammunition shells, mix them with water and eat it as porridge. 
The recipe below has been based on a recipe used during World War 1.
Ingredients (makes six biscuits)
• 190 g white flour 
• 375 g wholemeal flour 
• 40 g sugar 
• 21 g milk powder 
• good pinch salt 
• 220 ml water

water is 220 ml.

In 1898 one Lady Superintendent and 24 nurses formed the Army Nursing Service. This later 
became the Royal Australian Army Nursing Corps (RAANC). The RAANC were formed to care for 
Australian soldiers in times of war and its aftermath. The first group of nurses left Australia in

In September 1914, during World War 1, the first nurses left Australia. The nurses went 
wherever Australian and British troops served. Approximately 2140 served overseas, 420 
served in Australia, 25 died and 390 were decorated.

Red Cross 
5
Australian Red Cross was formed on 13 August 1914 exactly nine days after the outbreak of World 
War I. Lady Munro-Ferguson, who had worked for British Red Cross in Scotland and was the wife of 
the Governor-General, called on the wives of each State Governor to form a local committee in each 
capital. The women readily agreed and so Australian Red Cross was born.
During World War 2, Red Cross transported 40 000 pairs of socks, 25 000 shirts, 20 000 
underpants, 10 000 pairs of shoes and boots, 10 000 pairs of pyjamas, 5000 overcoats and 
many other items people thought would be useful to soldiers on the front in Europe. The effort 
from many small communities ‘beggared the imagination’. By the end of the war Red Cross 
unit of Rutherglen had forwarded, among many other items, more than 1200 shirts, 8500 
pairs of underpants, 1200 pairs of pyjamas, 2400 pairs of socks, 75 sheets, 770 pillow-cases, 
450 bed sheets and 390 handkerchiefs.

collect funds. Australian Red Cross volunteers despatched nearly 400 000 food parcels and

The Kokoda Trail

In World War 2, the Japanese army had advanced through Asia en route to Australia. Port Moresby, 
the capital of Papua New Guinea, was a significant base for both armies. Had the Japanese set up 
base in Port Moresby the Australian mainland would have been under severe threat of invasion. 
The Kokoda track was a seldom-used trail from the small coastal village of Buna on the north coast 
of Papua over the Owen Stanley Ranges to Port Moresby, passing through the village of Kokoda. In 
1942 the Japanese tried to capture Port Moresby by sea attack and then overland through Kokoda. 
The seven-month resistance of this ultimately unsuccessful campaign is regarded by some as one of 
the most heroic defensive actions in military history by an Australian force.

The Rats of Tobruk 
8
During World War 2, North Africa became a place of strategic importance to the Allied and German 
forces due to its position as a supply route. The Allied forces in North Africa included troops from 
Britain, Australia, New Zealand, United States and India. German troops were joined in their fight 
against the Allied forces by the Italian army.
• September 1940: Germans invade 
Egypt 
• January 1941: Australians capture 
Tobruk and its port 
• March 1941: Germans defeat 
Australians at El Agheila in Libya
• April 1941: Germans capture Libya 
(except for Tobruk) 
• April 1941: Germans attack Tobruk
• June 1942: Germans threaten Egypt
• May 1943: The Allied forces evict 
Germans from Africa
1 
Draw a timeline to 
represent these events.
2 
Colour the countries 
and the seas on the 
map.

in the campaign, the 
British and Australians

totalled more than 18 500. 
3

4

a Britain and Australia 
b United States 
c Germany and Italy.
5

The British and Australians won a decisive victory over the German and Italian forces at El 
Alamein in Egypt. The Germans and Italians had a total of 110 000 men and 500 tanks. The 
Allies had more than 200 000 men and more than 1000 tanks. This battle cost the Allied 
forces nearly 13 500 men; Germans and Italians lost 25 000 soldiers. The battle lasted for 13 
days.
6 
How many days (inclusive) did the battle last?
7 
Calculate the total number of soldiers killed.
8 
On average, how many soldiers were killed per day in the:
a Allied forces? 
b German and Italian Army?
9

a Allied forces 
b German and Italian Army.

‘Operation Supercharge’ was an attack by British and New Zealand troops against the forces 
of Rommel – the leader of the German and Italian Army in North Africa. 124 tanks attacked 
the German lines but 75% of them were lost in a sandstorm.
11 How many tanks were destroyed by the German Army? How many tanks were left?
The Allied forces began damaging the supply lines to Rommel so that only 33% of what 
Rommel needed was getting through to him. During June he received 5000 tonnes of supplies 
compared with 34 000 in May and 400 vehicles compared with 2000 in May.

described the Australians as ‘caught like rats in a trap’. The Australians managed to hold off 
the German forces for 250 days.

days in a month)?

special rule read ‘Play to be continuous until 1800 hours, except by interference by air raids. 
Play will NOT, rpt NOT cease during shell fire.’

Little Boy and Fat Man

During the final stages of World War 2, the United States dropped two atomic bombs over the 
Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in a successful attempt to hasten the end of the war. The 
nuclear weapon known as ‘Little Boy’ was dropped over Hiroshima on August 6 1945. ‘Fat Man’ was 
released over Nagasaki on August 9 of the same year.
The capture of Tinian, one of the Marianas Islands, provided American forces with a valuable 
airstrip from which to mount raids on Japan. The islands served as the base from which the 
atomic bomb attacks on Hiroshima and Nagasaki were staged.

b Nagasaki

bombing mission on August 6. A B-29 bomber was 
launched from Tinian in the west Pacific, about six 
hours flight time from Japan. Two other B-29s were also 
launched. After leaving Tinian the aircraft made their 
way separately to Iwo Jima where they met at an altitude 
of 2440 metres and set course for Japan. The aircraft 
arrived over the target in clear visibility at 9855 metres.

a   Iwo Jima? 
b  Hiroshima?

The gravity bomb known as ‘Little Boy’ was released at 8.15 am from a height of  
 
9855 metres.  ‘Little Boy’ contained 60 kilograms of uranium-235 and took 57 seconds to 
fall from the aircraft to the predetermined detonation height about 600 m above the city. 
It created a blast equivalent to about 13 kilotons of TNT. The uranium-235 weapon was 
considered very inefficient, with only 1.38% of its material exploding.

At the time of the attack the population of Hiroshima was approximately 345 000. 
Approximately 80 000 people were killed immediately and another 70 000 were injured. It has 
been estimated that, of the people who died on the day of the explosion, 60% died from burns, 
30% from falling bricks, timber and other materials and 10% from other causes.

immediately by the blast?

a  flash or flame burns? 
b falling debris?

On the morning of August 9 1945, the nuclear bomb code-named Fat Man was detonated. 
The bomb contained 6.4 kg of plutonium-239, and was dropped on Nagasaki’s industrial 
valley at 11.01 am. The estimated population of Nagasaki at the time of the bombing was 270 
000. Fat Man exploded 43 seconds later at 469 m above the ground. 
21 What was the time when Fat Man exploded?
22 Using the 24-hour clock, what time was Fat Man dropped?

60 000 people were killed in the blast.

On August 15, six days after the detonation over Nagasaki, Japan announced its surrender to 
the Allied Powers. They signed the Instrument of Surrender on September 2, officially ending 
the Pacific War and therefore World War 2.
25 After the bombing of Nagasaki, how many hours did it take for the Japanese to 
surrender?

The war on terror begins 
14
The War on Terror was launched following the terrorist attacks on the United States on September 
11 2001. It is a war against any terrorist activities or organisations and is supported by the United 
States, United Kingdom and many other countries.
The World Trade Center was constructed in the 
1960s. The two main towers had 110 stories and 
were 410 m high, with 920 m2 of office space. On 
completion in 1972 the North Tower became the 
tallest building in the world, a record it held for 
two years. It stood 417 m tall and featured a 110 m 
telecommunications antenna at the top, making 
the tower 527 m tall. 
On completion in 1973 the South Tower became 
the second tallest building in the world. Its rooftop 
was 420 m high. Each tower was 63.4 m2 at the 
base. The Leaning Tower of Pisa stands at 55.86 m 
and has a diameter of 15.5 m.

a  How many metres is this?  
b It is approximately 400 m around an 
athletics track. How many times would 
the cable used in the towers go around 
the track?

Knots and naughty miles 
16
World War 1 was largely fought and won on land but this could not have taken place without the 
movement of ships. Ships were used to transport supplies and manpower needed on the battlefields 
from overseas countries. Command of the seas and supply lines was essential to the armed forces 
on land.
The nautical mile is based on the circumference of the planet Earth. If you divide the circle 
made by the equator into 360 degrees and then divide a degree into 60 minutes, a single 
minute of arc on the planet Earth is 1 nautical mile. The nautical mile NM is a non-SI unit 
used mainly by navigators in the shipping and aviation industries.

The device that sailors used to make their measurement of speed was a rope with knots tied 
at equal distances along it, tied to a chip of wood. The sailor would throw the chip of wood 
over the side and when the chip was in the water they would start to count the number of 
knots that passed over the back of the ship in thirty seconds. This was the speed the ship was 
travelling. The knot is defined as one nautical mile per hour.

a  10 knots pass in 30 seconds? 
b 15 knots pass in one minute?
8

A guided missile is a self-propelled rocket used as a weapon. Missiles are propelled by a jet engine 
and generally have one or more explosive warheads. In military terms, the word missile describes a 
powered, guided munition, whilst the word rocket describes a powered, unguided munition. 
A cruise missile is basically a small, pilotless airplane. Cruise missiles have a 2.6-metre 
wingspan, are powered by turbofan engines and can fly 800 to 1600 kilometres, depending on 
their design.

Ballistic and Stinger missiles 
19
A ballistic missile is a munition that follows a parabolic 
flight path; it is a guided missile. Stinger missiles can be 
launched by foot soldiers. To fire the weapon, the soldier 
aims the missile at the target and the seeker locks on. 
Upon firing, a small launch rocket shoots the missile out

Grid references are used by many people including the armed forces to locate places of interest 
particularly on maps. Grids lines are placed on maps and labelled with sequential numbers or letters 
to provide a reference to features on the map. The numbers or letters are known as grid references. 
For example, Geranium is located in D3.

Factorising is writing an expression as a product of its factors. It is one way of simplifying an expression

Polynomial equations over the complex field have the form

Every polynomial equation of degree n > 0 with complex coefficients has n complex solutions (including repeated ones).

decay. Setting up the differential equation is half the task, the other half being to solve it under the given

Kinematics is an application of Calculus to the motion of particles. There are some key words and 
definitions ideas that will help you work out what a question is asking for and what information is given.

22 – Checklist for success 
Revision time
Done 
✓
I have tried all my homework and asked the 
teacher about any problem areas.
I have made a revision plan by dividing the 
course into blocks of time and have worked 
hard to stick to it.
My revision plan includes recreation and 
relaxation.
My revision plan includes a couple of free 
times in case I need to catch up because of 
sickness, etc.
I have altered my revision plan if I need to 
(sickness, etc.) immediately I needed to and 
not waited until the end.
I have helped myself learn by making my own 
notes of important points with examples, and 
organising a summary of the work in my own 
words.
I have thought about key ideas and methods, 
learned formulae, made summary tables and/
or mind maps.
I have ticked off my list of things as I have 
revised and always look at how much I’ve 
done rather than how much I have left to do.
I have rewarded myself each time I reach a 
target by going to the refrigerator or watching 
TV or calling a friend.
I have moved to the next topic knowing that 
I can talk to myself about the definitions of 
terms, the key points, real examples, formulae 
and graphs.
I know what sorts of questions I am likely to 
be asked: short answer/multichoice/…
I have practised each type of exam question 
(theory, skills, interpret, analyse)
I know what to do with questions with several 
parts.
I have worked through at least the last 2 year’s 
exams against the clock in the required time 
using only the tools I am allowed to use in the 
real exam.
I have had practice working for 2–3 hours 
without a break like I will need to do in the 
exam.
I have worked out how long each type of 
question should take by dividing the total 
exam time for each type by the number of 
questions.
I have checked that I have an approved calcu-
lator and spare batteries.
I know what will be on the formula sheet 
provided.
I have checked that I have pencils, pens,  
highlighters, ruler, eraser and other math-
ematical equipment.
I know what written notes (if allowed) and 
other things I can take into the exam.
I have a watch or clock I can use.
I have checked when the exam is on and 
where.
I have worked out how long it takes to travel 
to the exam and how I will travel.
The night before the exam
Done 
✓
I have put together what I need for the exams: 
calculator, spare batteries, pencils, pens, 
highlighters, written notes (if allowed), ruler, 
eraser and other mathematical equipment, 
and a watch or clock.
I have put out the clothes I need.
I have not done any more questions or tried to 
'cram', but have just read through my notes to 
refresh my memory and looked at questions I 
have already done correctly.
I have checked the length of the paper and 
worked out how long I should spend on each 
question.
I keep telling myself how much I know and 
understand.
I have double-checked when the exam is and 
where.
Everyone works differently so you should change this checklist to suit yourself and add some other things 
if you like. The important thing is to have a plan. That way you are less likely to put off the things you find 
hard. Finally, don’t stress about a problem, do something about it: spend more time on it or see the teacher.

Spend the correct amount of time on each 
question and go on to the next one even if I 
haven’t quite finished because I know I will 
have most of the marks for the answer by then 
anyway.
Return to unfinished questions after I have  
attempted all the questions I need to.
Try to write something down if I have a men-
tal block because I know that writing down 
a few relevant facts, equations or formulae, 
will probably jog my memory enough to get 
started (and I won’t get any marks for a blank 
sheet of paper).
Never leave out answers to multiple choice or 
short answer questions. I will have a go since 
there are no marks lost for wrong answers and 
I won’t get marks for gaps!
Always try to ask myself 'What does the 
examiner want?'
Answer the question asked, not the one I 
think was asked.
Use the method the examiner has said to use 
(if specified).
Give the answer in the form the examiner has 
asked for (if specified).
Reread the question when I have finished to 
make sure I have answered the question
Be extra careful with questions that I find easy 
because I may not think carefully enough.
Watch out for key words like 'hence' (use 
something done or given in an earlier part) 
and 'show' (prove or demonstrate).
Not use the calculator when the question asks 
for exact answers.
Use estimation to check my answer is sensible.
Use my calculator wisely, making sure that I 
put in brackets where I need them, that I am 
in the right mode (radian/degree).
If I have a graphing calculator, always adjust 
the window so I can see the key features of 
any graph. 
If I have a graphing calculator, use the CALC 
and not the TRACE button.
Take care to not make arithmetic and 
algebraic mistakes.
Round my numerical answer at the end rather 
than during the working.
Show all my working.
Make sure my answers are written legibly and 
logically.
Make sure I have put units on the answers if 
necessary.
Above all, take the chance I have been given 
to show the examiner what I know and 
understand and will feel confident that I have 
done my best, whatever my mark.

volume of the solid of revolution (or method of discs).

24 – Simple harmonic motion 
There are many other examples of using Newton’s Laws of Motion to solve problems. Check with your 
teacher to make sure that simple harmonic motion is on your syllabus.
1 
A particle P moves in a straight line such that its  
position at time t is given by x = 4 + sin3t – 3cos3t.
a Express sin3t – 3cos3t in the form Rsin(3t – α).
b Hence write down an expression for x in terms of 
Rsin(3t – α).
c The particle P is undergoing simple harmonic 
motion. Find the amplitude and the centre of the 
motion of P.
d Sketch a graph of 2 cycles of the motion.
e Find the time after t = 0 when P first reaches its maximum speed.
2 
A particle P is undergoing simple harmonic motion on 
the x-axis about the origin. The amplitude of the motion 
is 5 units and P returns to its initial position every  
2 seconds. If the particle is initially at its extreme  
positive position:
a write down the equation for the position of the  
particle at time t seconds
b find the time the particle will take to move from its rest 
position to the point halfway between the rest position  
and its equilibrium position.
3 
A small naval target of height 4 m rises and falls with the 
waves with simple harmonic motion of period 7 sec, the 
height of the waves from crest to trough being 8 m.  
a Explain why the height of the target above the trough is 
given by y = 4 + 8sin
2π 
7 t.
b The target can only be seen by a ship 5000 m away when it is at least  
6 m above the trough. Show that there is only a gap of approximately  
2.95 seconds of the cycle in which the target can be seen.
c A gun on the ship is aimed so that the centre of the target would be hit  
if the target stayed stationary in its topmost position. The bullet travels 
with a horizontal velocity of 2500 ms–1. By how much will the bullet miss 
the target? Assume that the ship is not rising and falling with the waves.
hint
Translate the words into mathematical 
form and don’t differentiate the 
expression first. Be careful to choose the 
correct value of x. Remember that the 
velocity is not constant. 
things to know
For simple harmonic motion (SHM) with displacement x(t) after time t, amplitude a and frequency f, x(t) = asin(2πft + α).  
If there is no displacement at time t = 0 then the phase α is zero. The period T of the motion is given by T = 1 
f .
Alternatively, the equation for simple harmonic motion can be written as x(t) = asin(nt + α) where the angular frequency 
n =2πf. Using differentiation it can be shown that v (t) = an cos(nt + α) and a(t) = -an2sin(nt + α) = -n2x(t), the condition 
for SHM. It is recommended that you use the correct terminology for centre, amplitude and period rather than personal 
notation that may be hard for the examiner to interpret.
trap

to find α. The centre of motion is not the time.

maximum speed. Remember to solve the equations 
completely before you discard values.

terminology. You have learned the formula  
x = a sin(nt + α) or x = a cos(nt + α) but what do 
they mean? What are a, n and α in this case?
hint
You should draw a 
diagram or graph to show 
the situation. Period and 
frequency should not be 
confused and be careful of 
your Algebra. Your calculator 
should be set to radians.

Factorising is writing an expression as a product of its factors. It is one way of simplifying an expression 
and is a necessary skill in the solution of many mathematical problems. Factorising over Q gives factors 
containing only rational numbers, while factorising over R gives factors containing irrational numbers as  
well. Expanding usually means multiplying out brackets. If you know about the Binomial Theorem, you  
can use that instead of multiplying. Some calculators can be used to factorise and expand expressions.  
The main thing is to be careful of slips in your work and practise, practise, practise.

5 – Solving equations and inequations 
The solution of equations is a necessary skill in Mathematics. It is particularly useful for finding intercepts 
when drawing graphs. Many algebraic equations can be solved by factorising and then using the ‘null factor 
law’: if the product of any two numbers is zero, then one or both of the numbers is zero. Absolute value 
functions and inequations require care with the positive and negative signs. The main thing is to be careful 
of slips in your work. Remember that another word for ‘solution’ of an equation is ‘root’ of the equation.

Know the facts about the properties of polynomial graphs! The domain is R. The graph will generally have one less 
turning point than the degree of the polynomial (y = x 3 has 2, y = x 4 has 3, etc.). Odd numbers of repeated factors 
may give inflection points. Repeated roots give ‘touchers’.
1

and hence the gradient of the graph.

things to know
Degree 1: linear function (straight line)
y = mx + c has gradient m and y-intercept c
Degree 2: quadratic function (parabola)
y = ±a(x – b)2 + c has turning point at (b, c) and 
y-intercept at (0, c ± ab 2)
y = ±a(x – h)(x – k) has x-intercepts at x = h and x = k 
Degree 3: cubic function
y = ±a(x – b)3 + c has inflection point at (b, c)  
y = ±a(x – h)(x – k)(x – ℓ) has x-intercepts at x = h, x = k 
and x = ℓ 
Degree 4: quartic function
y = ±a(x – b)4 + c has turning point at (b, c).
y = ±a(x – h)(x – k)(x – ℓ)(x – m) has x-intercepts at x = h,  
x = k, x = ℓ and x = m
y = ±a(x – h)2(x – k)(x – ℓ) has x-intercepts at x = h 
(touch), x = k and x = ℓ
y = ±a(x – h)3(x – k) has x-intercepts at x = h (inflection) 
and x = k

recognise them.

the value of x for which the minimum occurs.

which the maximum occurs.

at (–2, –9), (2, –9) and (0, 7). Use f''(x) or otherwise to identify the nature of the each of the turning points.

Certainly you should check to see whether the question is wanting the maximum/minimum value or the value of 
the variable for which it occurs. You will usually need to differentiate a function if it is a local maximum/minimum. 
You will need to confirm that you have a maximum or minimum or just an inflection point. (Do this by either

21 – Checklist for success 
Revision time
Done  
✓
I have tried all my homework and asked the 
teacher about any problem areas.
I have made a revision plan by dividing the course 
into blocks of time and have worked hard to stick 
to it.
My revision plan includes recreation and 
relaxation.
My revision plan includes a couple of free times in 
case I need to catch up because of sickness, etc.
I have altered my revision plan (sickness, etc.) 
immediately when I needed to and not waited until 
the end.
I have helped myself learn by making my own 
notes of important points with examples, and 
organising a summary of the work in my own 
words.
I have thought about key ideas and methods, 
learned formulae, made summary tables and/or 
mind maps.
I have ticked off my list of things as I have revised 
and always look at how much I’ve done rather than 
how much I have left to do.
I have rewarded myself each time I reached a target 
by going to the refrigerator or watching TV or 
calling a friend.
I have moved to the next topic knowing that I can 
talk to myself about the definitions of terms, the 
key points, real examples, formulae and graphs.
I know what sorts of questions I am likely to be 
asked: short answer, multiple choice, …
I have practised each type of exam question: 
theory, skills, interpret, analyse, …
I know what to do with questions with several 
parts.
I have worked through at least the last two year’s 
exams against the clock in the required time using 
only the tools I am allowed to use in the real exam.
I have had practice working for 2–3 hours without 
a break like I will need to do in the exam.
I have worked out how long each type of question 
should take by dividing the total exam time for 
each type by the number of questions.
I have checked that I have an approved calculator 
and spare batteries.
I know what will be on the formula sheet provided.
I have checked that I have pencils, pens, 
highlighters, ruler, eraser and other mathematical 
equipment.
I know what written notes (if allowed) and other 
things I can take into the exam.
I have a watch or clock I can use.
I have checked when the exam is on and where.
I have worked out how long it takes to travel to the 
exam and how I will travel.
The night before the Exam
Done  
✓
I have put together what I need for the exams: 
calculator, spare batteries, pencils, pens, 
highlighters, written notes (if allowed), ruler, 
eraser and other mathematical equipment, and a 
watch or clock.
I have put out the clothes I need.
I have not done any more questions or tried to 
‘cram’, but have just read through my notes to 
refresh my memory and looked at questions I have 
already done correctly.
I have checked the length of the paper and worked 
out how long I should spend on each question.
I keep telling myself how much I know and 
understand.
I have double-checked when the exam is and 
where.
I have double-checked my alarm clock (mechanical 
and human) to give myself plenty of time.
Everyone works differently so you should change this checklist to suit yourself and add some other things 
if you like. The important thing is to have a plan. That way you are less likely to put off the things you find 
hard. Finally, don’t stress about a problem, do something about it: spend more time on it or see the teacher.

I will

During the Exam – Good Habits
I will 
✓
Use my reading time to read the paper carefully, 
set times for different questions/sections and to 
work out which questions I will do first and which 
ones I think are harder and need to be done later 
in the exam.
Spend the correct amount of time on each question 
and go on to the next one even if I haven’t quite 
finished because I know I will have most of the 
marks for the answer by then anyway.
Remember that 1 mark means a mark for the 
answer only and more marks mean more work.
Return to unfinished questions after I have 
attempted all the questions I need to.
Try to write something down if I have a mental 
block because I know that writing down a few 
relevant facts, equations or formulae, will probably 
jog my memory enough to get started (and I won’t 
get any marks for a blank sheet of paper).
Never leave out answers to multiple choice or short 
answer questions. I will have a go since there are 
no marks lost for wrong answers and I won’t get 
marks for gaps!
Always try to ask myself ‘What does the examiner 
want?’
Answer the question asked, not the one I think was 
asked.
Use the method the examiners have said to use (if 
they have).
Give the answer in the form the examiners have 
asked for (if they have).
Reread the question when I have finished to make 
sure I have answered the question.
Be extra careful with questions that I find easy 
because I may not think carefully enough.
Watch out for key words like ‘hence’ (use 
something done or given in an earlier part) and 
‘show’ (prove or demonstrate).
Not use the calculator when the question asks for 
exact answers.
Use my calculator wisely, making sure that I put in 
brackets where I need them, that I am in the right 
mode (radian/degree).
If I have a graphical calculator, always adjust the 
window so I can see the key features of any graph. 
If I have a graphical calculator, use the CALC and 
not the TRACE button.
Take care to avoid making arithmetic and algebraic 
mistakes.
Show all my working.
Make sure my answers are written legibly and 
logically.
Above all, take the chance I have been given to 
show the examiner what I know and understand 
and will feel confident that I have done my best, 
whatever my mark.

10 – Probability and events 
You need to understand the basic principles of probability as well as be able to 
complete problems involving the concepts of dependent, independent, mutually 
exclusive, and conditional probability.  
Sometimes Venn or tree diagrams can be helpful.
things to know
Mutually exclusive events A and B do  
not intersect and so:  
Pr(A ∪ B ) = Pr(A) + Pr(B ). 
Non-mutually exclusive events A and B  
intersect and so: 
Pr(A ∪ B ) = Pr(A) + Pr(B ) – Pr(A ∩ B ).
If the event B is a subset of event A then Pr(A ∩ B ) = Pr(B ).
If events A and B are independent then  
Pr(A ∩ B ) = Pr(A) × Pr(B ).
If events A and B are dependent then   
Pr(A ∩ B ) = Pr(A|B ) × Pr(B ) and  
Pr(A ∩ B ) = Pr(A) × Pr(B |A). 
So Pr(B |A) = Pr(A ∩ B )
Pr(A)

probability the event B occurs given or knowing that event 
A has occurred. 
Remember that the probability of ‘not B’ is  
Pr(B ' ) = 1– Pr(B ).

13 – Probability and selections 
Some students will call these questions Hypergeometric Probability questions, and will use a formula.  
Some will work them out by first principles or with a tree diagram. You should try these questions  
using the method that your teacher suggests. Notice that there are lots of traps in these questions  
so read them carefully.
1 
Of the 20 students in the Year 12 Mathematics class, only 2 do not have a computer at home.  
If 5 students are selected at random, what is the probability, correct to 4 decimal places, that:
a only 3 of them have a computer at home?
 
 
 
 
 
b no more than one does not have a computer? 
 
 
 
 
 
2 
In a draw of raffle tickets numbered from 1 to 99, two lucky numbers are 
selected at the same time at random from a hat.
a In how many ways can the two lucky numbers be selected?
 
 
 
 
 
b John bought two tickets in this raffle. What is the probability that at least one of his two numbers will be 
selected?
 
 
 
 
 
3 
I always buy the same socks and only ever buy either white or  
black. At the moment there are 6 pairs of black socks and 4 pairs  
of white socks in my drawer. When I got up this morning in the 
dark I grabbed two individual socks. What is the exact value of  
the probability that they matched?
 
 
 
 
 
4 
Packets of printing paper come in reams (500 sheets) which are then 
packed in boxes. A number of boxes of printing paper was stained by 
water in a recent flood. If a random sample of 3 reams of paper was 
selected from a box of 12 reams in which 4 reams were stained, what  
is the probability that at least one ream was stained?
 
 
 
 
 
5 
The local school decided to hold a lucky draw with 450 tickets being 
sold. 150 tickets were pink, 150 were yellow and 150 were blue and 
there were to be three lucky tickets drawn. Winning tickets were not 
replaced before the next ticket was drawn. Find the probability, correct 
to 3 significant figures, that:
a each of the winning tickets is pink.
 
 
 
 
 
b all the tickets are of different colours.
 
 
 
 
 
c at least one of the winning tickets is not blue.
 
 
 
 
 
trap
Watch the sneaky wording!
trap
Read the question carefully: ‘pairs 
of socks’ and ‘individual socks’. 
This is the sort of trap you should 
notice during reading time. And 
‘exact value’ means no decimals.
hint
‘At the same time’ is like 
‘without replacement’.
hint
Note the difference between 
‘only one stained’ (= 1) and  
‘at least one stained’ ( 1).
hint
Notice that the tickets 
are not replaced before the 
next draw, so the probability 
changes for each draw. Also 
make sure you show all of 
your working: sometimes an 
answer is approximately the 
same as the correct answer 
and the examiner needs 
to know how you got your 
answer. Read the question 
carefully, like ‘not blue’.

9, while if the first card is black then the probability that the second card

3 .

Boxes of sultanas are labelled as containing 250 g. In fact, 
the weight of the contents is normally distributed with mean 
250.5 g and standard deviation 0.75 g. Find the proportion of 
boxes on the supermarket shelves that contain less than the 
labelled weight of sultanas.

number mark a student needs to get a B?

heights of students entering a first year course. Over the long term  
it was found that the heights were normally distributed with mean

students are between 159 cm and 192 cm tall?

standard deviation 6 cm. If the distribution of babies’ lengths is

 ii will be less than $500.

17 – Sequences and series 
Number patterns are useful in many branches of mathematics. You need to know the rules for finding the 
general term or sum of a sequence of numbers. As usual, real life examples can have ‘yucky’ formulae but 
they are not necessarily difficult. If this topic is not in your syllabus this year, you can still complete most of 
the questions just because they give you good practice in your algebra and arithmetic.

Gen the librarian has been wondering whether the number of pages in a book affects how often the book is 
borrowed. From her records, she finds that 6.5% of borrowed books have about 125 pages.
a Of the 4250 books borrowed this week, how many would she expect to have about 125 pages?
 
 
 
 
 
b Of the 1050 books borrowed by the Year 9 class, how many would she expect to have other than  
about 125 pages?
 
 
 
 
 
3 
In a particular town there are people with four different hair colours: blonde, 
brunette, redhead and ‘mouse’. The probabilities of these particular hair colours  
are shown in the table. 
a Knowing that the sum of the probabilities of these events is 1, show that x  
must be a solution to the quadratic equation 9x 2 + 8x – 1 = 0.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
b Hence find the exact value of x.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
c Use substitution for the value of x to find the probability of a randomly selected person being a redhead.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The expected value of an event can be found by multiplying the probability of that event by the number of trials.
d If a sample of 8 people is selected at random, how many would be expected to be redhead?  
Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

This should ideally be done towards the end of the year when all the topics have been consolidated.
